metadata.title: Epilepsies in children, young people and adults
quality_flags: The document describes changes dated November 2025 although its stated last-update date is 30 January 2025.
metadata.summary: This guideline addresses the diagnosis, assessment and management of epilepsy across childhood, adolescence and adulthood, including referral between primary, secondary and tertiary services. It covers treatment by seizure type and epilepsy syndrome, emergency seizure management, medication safety, monitoring and withdrawal, and non-pharmacological options. It also addresses comorbidities, support during pregnancy and transition to adult services, and reduction of epilepsy-related mortality.

conditions_covered: focal seizures with or without evolution to bilateral tonic-clonic seizures
glucose transporter type 1 deficiency syndrome (GLUT1 deficiency syndrome)
epilepsy associated with pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency
seizures caused by tuberous sclerosis complex
seizures caused by cyclin-dependent kinase-like 5 (CDKL5) deficiency disorder
target_population: children, young people and adults with suspected or confirmed epilepsy
people after a first suspected seizure or seizure recurrence after remission
women and girls with epilepsy who are planning pregnancy or are pregnant
men with epilepsy who are planning a family
people with epilepsy and mental health conditions, learning disabilities or other complex needs

prevention: Recognise the increased risk associated with phenytoin in people of Han Chinese or Thai family background.

Recognise the increased risk associated with carbamazepine, and potentially with medicines of similar chemical structure such as oxcarbazepine and eslicarbazepine acetate, in people of Han Chinese, Thai, European or Japanese family background.

toxicities.event: Reduced bone mineral density and osteomalacia
prevention: Follow MHRA safety advice on the adverse effects of antiepileptics on bone, and consider vitamin D and calcium supplementation for people at risk.

toxicities.event: Congenital malformations, neurodevelopmental impairments and fetal growth restriction
prevention: Discuss risks to an unborn child with women and girls who can have children, including younger girls likely to require treatment during their childbearing years. When prescribing, weigh the risks and benefits of each antiseizure medication using the latest safety data, while acknowledging important uncertainty, particularly for newer medicines.
Discuss the pregnancy risks of sodium valproate specifically, including the increased risk with higher doses and polytherapy, and those of topiramate.
Do not use sodium valproate or topiramate in women and girls of childbearing potential unless the conditions of the Pregnancy Prevention Programme are fulfilled.

Refer women and girls with epilepsy who are pregnant or planning pregnancy to an epilepsy specialist team to review antiseizure medication options. Discuss medication changes in the context of both poorly controlled seizures and potential risks to the baby.

toxicities.event: Possible neurodevelopmental disorders in children following paternal sodium valproate exposure around conception
recognition: The association is possible; whether sodium valproate has a causal role is unknown.
prevention: Advise boys and men to use effective contraception consisting of condoms plus contraception used by a female sexual partner throughout treatment and for 3 months after stopping valproate.
Refer men taking sodium valproate who plan a family within the next year to an epilepsy specialist team to review medication options and discuss potential fertility risks.

management.actions: Consult the SPC and BNF or BNF for children for advice specific to interactions between the individual antiseizure medication and contraception.

toxicities.event: Reduced effectiveness of lamotrigine with hormonal treatment
recognition: Oestrogen-containing hormonal contraceptives and hormone replacement therapy can reduce the effectiveness of lamotrigine.

toxicities.event: Potential effects of antiseizure medication on a breastfed child

management.actions: Prescribers should consult advice for the individual medicine in the SPC and BNF or BNF for children. Decide on treatment and breastfeeding together with the woman or girl, weighing breastfeeding benefits against possible medication effects on the child. Breastfeeding is generally safe for babies of most women and girls taking antiseizure medications and should be encouraged, while supporting each mother's choice of feeding method.

toxicities.event: Sedation and other adverse effects during add-on antiseizure treatment
recognition: Sedation is an adverse effect identified for monitoring during add-on treatment.

management.actions: Review treatment frequently and monitor adverse effects when adding an antiseizure medicine, including when using stiripentol and clobazam with sodium valproate for Dravet syndrome or starting add-on treatment for Lennox–Gastaut syndrome.

prevention: Titrate an added antiseizure medicine carefully.
toxicities.dose_modifications: When adding lamotrigine in Lennox–Gastaut syndrome, the committee recommends a lower initial dose and cautious titration because of its interaction with sodium valproate.

toxicities.event: Steroid-related infection risk, high blood pressure and high blood sugar
recognition: Increased susceptibility to infection, elevated blood pressure and elevated blood sugar are possible steroid-related effects.

management.severity: high risk of steroid-related side effects
management.actions: For infantile spasms, consider vigabatrin alone as first-line treatment.

prevention: Before treating infantile spasms with oral prednisolone, discuss possible steroid effects with parents or carers, check whether the child has antibodies to varicella zoster virus, and provide a steroid card and advice on when to seek medical help.
Provide parents and carers with information on limiting exposure to infections such as chickenpox and on what to do after possible exposure.

management.actions: If seizures recur during or after medication discontinuation, undo the most recent dose reduction and seek advice from an epilepsy specialist according to the agreed plan.

prevention: Agree an individualised discontinuation plan and reduce antiseizure medicines gradually. If several are prescribed, stop them one at a time.
toxicities.dose_modifications: For most antiseizure medicines, reduction would typically take at least 3 months; benzodiazepines and barbiturates would typically require a longer period to limit drug-related withdrawal symptoms.

prevention: The committee does not recommend ketogenic diets routinely; consider one under tertiary specialist guidance for the specified childhood-onset syndromes or when other options for drug-resistant epilepsy are unsuccessful or inappropriate.

toxicities.event: Perioperative infection, bleeding, postoperative cognitive deficits and mood changes
prevention: Explain the benefits and risks of surgical procedures when discussing assessment for resective epilepsy surgery.

prophylaxis.recommendation: Do not use sodium valproate or topiramate in women and girls of childbearing potential unless the conditions of the Pregnancy Prevention Programme are met. For sodium valproate, the guideline also specifies that other treatment options must be unsuitable and reproductive risks and benefits must be fully discussed. Programme measures include highly effective contraception and a pregnancy test to exclude pregnancy before starting either medicine.
prophylaxis.target_population: Women and girls of childbearing potential, including young girls likely to need treatment into their childbearing years

prophylaxis.recommendation: Advise the use of condoms together with contraception used by a female sexual partner.
prophylaxis.duration: Throughout the valproate treatment period and for 3 months after stopping valproate

prophylaxis.recommendation: Consider supplementation in accordance with MHRA advice concerning the effects of antiepileptics on bone.
prophylaxis.target_population: People at risk of decreased bone mineral density or osteomalacia during long-term antiseizure medication treatment

prophylaxis.recommendation: Before starting oral prednisolone for infantile spasms, check for antibodies to varicella zoster virus. Give parents or carers information on reducing infection exposure, including exposure to chickenpox, and on what to do if exposure may have occurred.
prophylaxis.target_population: Children starting oral prednisolone for infantile spasms and their parents or carers

prophylaxis.recommendation: Support people to take antiseizure medication as prescribed to reduce seizures and epilepsy-related death. Discuss individual risk factors for sudden unexpected death in epilepsy (SUDEP), including potentially modifiable factors, from diagnosis onwards.
prophylaxis.target_population: People with epilepsy; medication adherence is particularly important for those with generalised tonic-clonic seizures or focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizures

prophylaxis.recommendation: Discuss introducing or increasing night-time supervision; a parent or carer may wish to use a night monitor. Discuss SUDEP risk and ways to minimise it, including taking medication as prescribed.
prophylaxis.target_population: People who have seizures during sleep and have been assessed as being at higher risk of epilepsy-related death

infection_management.prevention: Before oral prednisolone is started for infantile spasms, test whether the child has antibodies to varicella zoster virus. Advise parents or carers on reducing exposure to infections such as chickenpox and on what to do after possible exposure.

therapies_index.name: carbamazepine
approved_indications: Second-line monotherapy and first-line add-on treatment for focal seizures.
Second-line monotherapy for self-limited epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes.
key_toxicities: Increased risk of serious skin reactions in people of Han Chinese, Thai, European or Japanese family background.
Long-term treatment is associated with reduced bone mineral density and an increased risk of osteomalacia.

May worsen seizures in people with absence, myoclonic, tonic or atonic seizures, Dravet syndrome or Lennox–Gastaut syndrome; it should not be used for myoclonic seizures or epilepsy with myoclonic-atonic seizures.
May rarely worsen seizures, contribute to another epilepsy syndrome or affect cognition in children and young people with self-limited epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes.
Can reduce the effectiveness of hormonal contraceptives.
monitoring: For pregnant people or those planning pregnancy who take carbamazepine, monitor and adjust dosage in accordance with MHRA advice.
If school performance raises concern during treatment for self-limited epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes, seek specialist advice and consider sleep EEG and neuropsychology assessment.

Second-line add-on treatment for focal seizures.

First-line treatment alone for infantile spasms due to tuberous sclerosis or when steroid-related adverse effects pose a high risk; first-line combination treatment with high-dose oral prednisolone for infantile spasms not due to tuberous sclerosis, unless steroid-related adverse effects pose a high risk.

key_toxicities: May aggravate absence, myoclonic, tonic or atonic seizures, or seizures in Dravet syndrome or Lennox–Gastaut syndrome; it should not be used for myoclonic seizures or epilepsy with myoclonic-atonic seizures.
monitoring: For infantile spasms, assess whether spasms have stopped clinically and on EEG; repeat sleep EEG at 2 weeks after starting treatment.

therapies_index.name: ethosuximide
approved_indications: First-line treatment for absence seizures.

approved_indications: An option for Dravet syndrome when all other treatments have not worked, under the guidance of a neurologist with expertise in epilepsy.
monitoring: Use under the guidance of a neurologist with expertise in epilepsy.

therapies_index.name: prednisolone
approved_indications: High-dose oral treatment with vigabatrin as first-line therapy for infantile spasms not due to tuberous sclerosis, unless steroid-related adverse effects pose a high risk.
An addition to vigabatrin for infantile spasms due to tuberous sclerosis if vigabatrin has not worked after 1 week.

therapies_index.name: triple therapy with stiripentol and clobazam
approved_indications: First-line add-on therapy for Dravet syndrome when sodium valproate alone has not worked.
key_toxicities: Sedation can occur with the added medicines.
monitoring: Titrate the additional medicines carefully and review treatment frequently, including for sedation.

therapies_index.name: high-dose oral prednisolone and vigabatrin
approved_indications: First-line combination treatment for infantile spasms not due to tuberous sclerosis, unless the child has a high risk of steroid-related adverse effects.
For infantile spasms due to tuberous sclerosis, add high-dose oral prednisolone if first-line vigabatrin alone has not worked after 1 week.

monitoring: Before oral prednisolone, test for antibodies to the varicella zoster virus and discuss steroid-related adverse effects with parents or carers.
Monitor blood pressure and urinary glucose weekly during oral prednisolone treatment.

therapies_index.name: ketogenic diet
approved_indications: An option under specialist guidance for certain childhood-onset epilepsies, including glucose transporter type 1 deficiency syndrome (GLUT1 deficiency syndrome), epilepsy associated with pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency, infantile spasms syndrome, epilepsy with myoclonic-atonic seizures (Doose syndrome), Dravet syndrome and Lennox–Gastaut syndrome.
An option for drug-resistant epilepsy when other treatments have not worked or are unsuitable.
A specified later-line option for tonic or atonic seizures in children, Dravet syndrome, Lennox–Gastaut syndrome, infantile spasms and epilepsy with myoclonic-atonic seizures.
therapies_index.administration: Use under the guidance of a tertiary epilepsy specialist or, where specified, the supervision of a ketogenic diet team.
key_toxicities: The committee noted potential long-term health drawbacks without specifying them.
monitoring: Specialist or ketogenic diet team supervision is specified for its use in the relevant treatment pathways.

therapies_index.name: resective epilepsy surgery
approved_indications: Consider assessment for people with drug-resistant epilepsy, including those without an identified MRI abnormality.
Consider early tertiary assessment when MRI abnormalities indicate a high risk of drug resistance.
therapies_index.administration: Adults are referred to a tertiary epilepsy service; children and young people are referred to a tertiary paediatric neurology service for consideration of assessment at a children's epilepsy service surgery centre.
key_toxicities: Potential harms include postoperative cognitive deficits, perioperative infection, bleeding and postoperative mood changes.
monitoring: After surgery, discontinue antiseizure medication under the guidance of the epilepsy surgery centre.

therapies_index.name: vagus nerve stimulation
approved_indications: Consider as an add-on to antiseizure medication for drug-resistant seizures when resective epilepsy surgery is unsuitable.
therapies_index.administration: Used as an add-on treatment alongside antiseizure medication.
key_toxicities: The procedure carries risks, but the guideline does not specify individual adverse events.

therapies_index.name: general anaesthesia
approved_indications: A third-line option under expert guidance for convulsive status epilepticus that has not responded to second-line treatments tried.
therapies_index.administration: Use under expert guidance; no specific regimen is provided.

conditions.name: Epilepsy
conditions.description: A condition requiring assessment of seizure type, epilepsy syndrome and possible cause. Treatment decisions depend on the individual's seizure pattern, circumstances and preferences.
conditions.epidemiology: Compared with the general population, people with epilepsy have more mental health difficulties, learning disabilities, neurodevelopmental conditions and dementia, as well as a greater risk of suicide and premature death. The estimated lifetime risk of sudden unexpected death in epilepsy (SUDEP) is between 7% and 12%.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess a suspected first seizure and support expert clinical diagnosis.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: After a first suspected seizure.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Eyewitness accounts and seizure videos can supplement, but not replace, specialist assessment.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify cardiac conditions that could resemble an epileptic seizure.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: After a first suspected seizure.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: An abnormal result may identify a cardiac cause; a normal result can support further investigation of suspected epilepsy.

diagnostic_workup.test: Assessment for metabolic disturbance, including hypoglycaemia
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Consider metabolic causes of seizures.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During assessment after a first suspected seizure.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate a possible structural cause.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When an underlying structural cause is suspected.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Neuroimaging alone did not have sufficient accuracy to serve as a diagnostic test for epilepsy.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Support diagnosis and help identify seizure type or epilepsy syndrome.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Consider when the history and examination suggest an epileptic seizure and epilepsy is suspected; if requested after a first seizure, perform as soon as possible, ideally within 72 hours.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A positive finding can support a provisional diagnosis; a normal EEG must not be used to rule out epilepsy.

diagnostic_workup.test: EEG with hyperventilation or photic stimulation
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Potentially increase information from a routine EEG.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: If the person agrees after discussion of benefits and risks.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A negative finding does not rule out epilepsy.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Provide further diagnostic information.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Consider after a normal routine EEG, subject to agreement following discussion of benefits and risks.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A normal finding does not exclude epilepsy.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate persisting diagnostic uncertainty.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Consider for up to 48 hours if routine and sleep-deprived EEG are normal and uncertainty remains.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Detect structural abnormalities relevant to cause, prognosis or management.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Offer after diagnosis unless the person has idiopathic generalised epilepsy or self-limited epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes; perform within 6 weeks of referral using regionally agreed epilepsy MRI protocols. Consider an additional scan if the original was suboptimal, new epilepsy features arise, specified syndromes do not respond to first-line treatment, or surgery is contemplated.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A radiologist with appropriate paediatric or adult neuroradiology expertise should report the scan. If seizures continue despite treatment and diagnosis remains uncertain, consider review at a tertiary centre.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Provide an imaging alternative when MRI cannot be performed.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Consider if MRI is contraindicated. Do not routinely perform after a typical seizure in someone with established epilepsy attending an emergency department unless another concern exists.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate an unknown cause of epilepsy.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Consider if onset was under 2 years, features suggest a specific genetic epilepsy syndrome, or additional features include a learning disability, autism spectrum disorder, a structural abnormality, or unexplained cognitive or memory decline. For onset between 2 and 3 years, consider if a specialist multidisciplinary team agrees.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Genetic results may inform treatment, associated medical problems, prognosis and counselling; discuss implications and obtain informed consent with appropriate genetic counselling before testing.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate possible autoimmune encephalitis.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Consider after discussion with a neurologist when epilepsy is newly diagnosed and autoimmune encephalitis is suspected; routine testing for everyone with epilepsy is not supported.

prognostic_tools.name: SUDEP-7
prognostic_tools.interpretation: Limited data suggested promising accuracy for predicting SUDEP, but estimates were highly imprecise because few events were recorded; the guideline does not recommend its use as a prediction tool.

prognostic_tools.name: SUDEP-7 revised
prognostic_tools.interpretation: Limited data suggested promising accuracy for predicting SUDEP, but estimates were highly imprecise because few events were recorded; the guideline does not recommend its use as a prediction tool.

follow_up.schedule: Arrange reviews at least annually for adults with a learning disability, drug-resistant epilepsy, high SUDEP risk, serious comorbidity, or use of medicines associated with long-term adverse effects or interactions, including specified teratogenic medicines in people able to become pregnant. Agree an individually tailored review schedule for children and young people, at least every 12 months. For ongoing seizures, offer epilepsy specialist nurse sessions at least twice a year and after emergency department visits.
recommended_tests: Consider antiseizure medication levels for uncontrolled seizures, adverse effects, poor adherence, or a condition requiring closer supervision, such as pregnancy or renal failure.
At routine reviews, assess neurodevelopment, cognition, mental health, social and emotional wellbeing, and learning disabilities.
long_term_effects: Some long-term antiseizure medication use is associated with reduced bone mineral density and osteomalacia.
Potential long-term medication effects noted for review include changes in blood parameters, bone health and lipid metabolism.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Discuss individual risks of epilepsy-related death, including SUDEP, from diagnosis onward. A person can request reassessment when concerns arise or care needs change.

conditions.name: Drug-resistant epilepsy
conditions.description: Epilepsy in which seizures persist and further changes to antiseizure medicines are very unlikely to achieve sustained seizure freedom. The International League Against Epilepsy definition requires unsuccessful adequate trials of 2 tolerated, appropriately selected and used antiseizure medication schedules, alone or in combination.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Seizures continue despite adequate antiseizure treatment.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Review diagnosis, cause, seizure type, syndrome and further treatment options.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Refer to a tertiary epilepsy service for assessment within 4 weeks when seizures are drug resistant or the syndrome is likely to be drug resistant.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess structural causes and inform possible surgical evaluation.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Consider an additional scan if surgery is under consideration; lack of an identified MRI abnormality does not preclude referral for surgical assessment.

follow_up.schedule: Adults with drug-resistant epilepsy should have regular reviews at least annually.
recommended_tests: Consider monitoring antiseizure medication levels when seizures are uncontrolled.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Discuss individual epilepsy-related mortality risk. Consider tertiary assessment for resective epilepsy surgery, including when MRI shows no abnormality.

conditions.name: Generalised tonic-clonic seizures
conditions.description: Seizures that rapidly affect both cerebral hemispheres.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Consciousness is lost, with muscular stiffening followed by rhythmic jerking.

follow_up.survivorship_notes: Uncontrolled generalised tonic-clonic seizures are highlighted as a potentially modifiable SUDEP risk factor.

conditions.name: Focal seizures with or without evolution to bilateral tonic-clonic seizures
conditions.description: Seizures beginning in 1 region of 1 cerebral hemisphere; they may evolve to bilateral tonic-clonic seizures.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Awareness may be preserved or impaired. Manifestations vary according to the region where the seizure begins.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Provide additional information when the diagnosis remains uncertain.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: The committee identified suspected focal epilepsy as a situation in which ambulatory monitoring may be particularly useful after normal routine and sleep-deprived EEG results.

follow_up.survivorship_notes: Focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizures are identified as a potentially modifiable SUDEP risk factor.

conditions.name: Absence seizures
conditions.description: A generalised seizure type that may occur alone or alongside other seizure types and epilepsy syndromes.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Episodes involve impaired awareness, interruption of movement or speech, and a fixed stare.

subtypes.name: childhood absence epilepsy
subtypes.distinguishing_features: A syndrome that can include absence seizures.

subtypes.name: juvenile absence epilepsy
subtypes.distinguishing_features: A syndrome that can include absence seizures.

conditions.name: Absence seizures with other seizure types
conditions.description: Absence seizures occurring with, or in someone at risk of, other seizure types; this distinction affects treatment selection.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Absence episodes may coexist with other seizure manifestations.

conditions.name: Myoclonic seizures
conditions.description: A generalised seizure type. Onset before 4 years may indicate an underlying neurodegenerative disorder.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Obtain guidance on diagnosis and treatment, including consideration of an underlying disorder.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When a child under 4 years has myoclonic seizures.

conditions.name: Tonic or atonic seizures
conditions.description: Generalised seizure types that can occur in Lennox–Gastaut syndrome or other epilepsy syndromes and aetiologies.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Atonic events involve a generalised loss of tone, whereas tonic events involve sustained generalised stiffening. Either can cause a sudden fall and injury.

diagnostic_workup.test: Assessment by a neurologist with expertise in epilepsy
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify the syndrome where possible and advise on investigations and treatment.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: After diagnosis of tonic or atonic seizures.

follow_up.survivorship_notes: Falls can cause injuries and substantially affect quality of life.

conditions.name: Idiopathic generalised epilepsies
conditions.description: A group of generalised epilepsies whose seizures often respond to antiseizure medication, with seizure freedom as the treatment goal.
conditions.epidemiology: Described as 1 of the most common forms of epilepsy. Onset is usually in adolescence, although childhood onset occurs.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Seizures may continue into middle age. Some evidence suggests subsequent remission, but which individuals will remit cannot be predicted.

subtypes.name: juvenile myoclonic epilepsy
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Mentioned among idiopathic generalised epilepsies and among syndromes in which absence or myoclonic seizures may occur.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate possible structural abnormalities if the expected treatment response does not occur.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Initial MRI is not routinely offered for this diagnosis; consider an additional MRI if first-line treatment fails.

follow_up.survivorship_notes: Stopping antiseizure medication in juvenile myoclonic epilepsy can carry a substantial risk of seizure recurrence.

conditions.name: Dravet syndrome
conditions.description: A complex epilepsy syndrome with variable treatment response; its diagnosis may be difficult during the first year of life.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Onset is usually in the first year of life. Children can present with prolonged febrile seizures that require intensive care.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Confirm and discuss the diagnosis and guide care.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When Dravet syndrome is suspected or diagnosed.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The syndrome-specific treatment recommendations apply once the diagnosis has been confirmed and discussed with a paediatric neurologist.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate a possible genetic cause of epilepsy.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Consider in epilepsy of unknown cause with clinical features suggesting a specific genetic syndrome, for which Dravet syndrome is given as an example.

follow_up.schedule: Review treatment frequently when additional medicines are introduced.
recommended_tests: Monitor for adverse effects, including sedation, during titration of add-on treatment.

conditions.name: Lennox–Gastaut syndrome
conditions.description: A severe developmental and epileptic encephalopathy beginning in childhood. Diagnosis and treatment can be difficult, and treatment response varies.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Tonic or atonic seizures and drop attacks can occur; antiseizure medication may be started before a final syndrome diagnosis is established.

diagnostic_workup.test: Assessment by an adult or paediatric neurologist with expertise in epilepsy
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Support diagnosis and guide care.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: For people with Lennox–Gastaut syndrome.

follow_up.schedule: Review treatment frequently when introducing add-on medication.
recommended_tests: Monitor for adverse effects such as sedation during careful add-on medicine titration.

conditions.name: Infantile spasms syndrome
conditions.description: A severe developmental and epileptic encephalopathy requiring urgent assessment and treatment. Without treatment, adverse long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes are a concern.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Infantile spasms in a child under 2 years warrant urgent specialist attention.

subtypes.name: infantile spasms due to tuberous sclerosis
subtypes.distinguishing_features: An underlying cause associated with a distinct first-line treatment approach.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Support rapid assessment and evaluate treatment response or possible recurrence.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Arrange urgent assessment for suspected or confirmed spasms in a child under 2 years; repeat at 2 weeks after starting treatment, and again if spasms return or clinical concerns arise.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Clinical findings and EEG are both used to assess whether spasms have stopped.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess antibody status before steroid treatment.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Before starting oral prednisolone.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Monitor adverse effects during oral prednisolone treatment.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Weekly throughout treatment with oral prednisolone.

follow_up.schedule: Review children under 2 years at least weekly during treatment. After spasms cease, review monthly.
recommended_tests: Repeat sleep EEG at 2 weeks after treatment starts.
Repeat sleep EEG if spasms recur or there are clinical concerns.
Check blood pressure and urinary glucose weekly during oral prednisolone treatment.
long_term_effects: Untreated spasms may be followed by poor neurodevelopmental outcomes.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Monitor during and after treatment for recurrent spasms, emergence of other seizure types and treatment-related adverse effects.

conditions.name: Self-limited epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes
conditions.description: A childhood epilepsy that generally resolves by the early teenage years. Some children have infrequent seizures with little effect on wellbeing.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Children and young people usually have focal seizures. In a small number, seizures or another epilepsy syndrome may emerge or worsen during certain treatments, or cognitive performance may be affected.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess whether another relevant abnormality is present if initial treatment does not work.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Initial MRI is not routinely offered for this syndrome; consider an additional scan when it does not respond to first-line treatment.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate worsening epileptic activity.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Consider if school performance raises concern or a child receiving antiseizure medication develops other seizure types.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: For school concerns, assess for electrical status epilepticus during sleep; with new seizure types, assess for developmental epileptic encephalopathy with spike-wave activation in sleep.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Review academic performance.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Consider if there are concerns about school performance during antiseizure medication treatment.

follow_up.schedule: Arrange follow-up at a frequency suited to the child or young person's needs. Discuss stopping treatment after at least 2 years without seizures or at age 14 years.
recommended_tests: Consider sleep EEG and neuropsychology assessment when school performance causes concern.
Consider sleep EEG if other seizure types develop during treatment.
long_term_effects: Carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine and lamotrigine may rarely worsen seizures, contribute to development of another epilepsy syndrome, or affect cognitive performance in a small number of children and young people.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Treatment is not chosen by every child or family; discussion should weigh seizure frequency and severity, hazards of continued seizures and possible treatment adverse effects.

conditions.name: Epilepsy with myoclonic-atonic seizures (Doose syndrome)
conditions.description: An epilepsy affecting young children for which accurate diagnosis is important to management. Children may outgrow their seizures by their teenage years.

diagnostic_workup.test: Discussion with a tertiary paediatric neurologist
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Obtain specialist advice on diagnosis, treatment and management.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: For affected children.

follow_up.schedule: Consider stopping antiseizure medication after 2 years without seizures.

conditions.name: Status epilepticus
conditions.description: Convulsive status epilepticus is an emergency requiring immediate resuscitation and treatment; the guideline identifies convulsive seizures lasting 5 minutes or more.
conditions.clinical_presentation: A continuing convulsive seizure may resemble a non-epileptic, dissociative seizure. Possible underlying contributors include hypoglycaemia, eclampsia, alcohol withdrawal and non-adherence to antiseizure medication.

subtypes.name: convulsive status epilepticus
subtypes.distinguishing_features: A convulsive seizure continuing for 5 minutes or more.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify contributors that may require additional treatment.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During emergency management of status epilepticus.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Consider hypoglycaemia, eclampsia, alcohol withdrawal and non-adherence; also consider whether the presentation is a non-epileptic seizure.

follow_up.schedule: After an episode, agree an individualised emergency plan if one is not already in place and recurrence is a concern.

conditions.name: Repeated seizures or cluster seizures
conditions.description: Typically 3 or more seizures that each stop spontaneously within 24 hours; manage the episode as a medical emergency.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Multiple self-terminating seizures occur over a short interval.

follow_up.schedule: Seek expert guidance for further episodes. After an episode, agree an individualised emergency plan if none exists and recurrence is a concern.

conditions.name: Prolonged seizures
conditions.description: The guideline distinguishes seizures that exceed a person's usual duration by more than 2 minutes from convulsive seizures lasting 5 minutes or more, which are managed as status epilepticus.
conditions.clinical_presentation: A convulsive or non-convulsive seizure continues for more than 2 minutes beyond that person's usual seizure duration.

subtypes.name: prolonged convulsive seizures
subtypes.distinguishing_features: A convulsive seizure lasting more than 2 minutes beyond the person's usual duration; manage as a medical emergency.

subtypes.name: prolonged non-convulsive seizure
subtypes.distinguishing_features: A non-convulsive seizure lasting more than 2 minutes beyond the person's usual duration.

follow_up.schedule: After a prolonged convulsive or non-convulsive seizure, agree an emergency plan if none exists and recurrence is a concern.

conditions.name: seizures caused by tuberous sclerosis complex
conditions.description: Childhood-onset seizures associated with tuberous sclerosis complex for which the guideline cites a specific add-on treatment option.

conditions.name: seizures caused by cyclin-dependent kinase-like 5 (CDKL5) deficiency disorder
conditions.description: Seizures associated with cyclin-dependent kinase-like 5 (CDKL5) deficiency disorder, addressed through a cited technology appraisal concerning children aged 2 years and over.

conditions.name: glucose transporter type 1 deficiency syndrome (GLUT1 deficiency syndrome)
conditions.description: Cited as an example of a childhood-onset epilepsy syndrome for which specialist consideration of a ketogenic diet may be appropriate.

conditions.name: epilepsy associated with pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency
conditions.description: Cited as an example of childhood-onset epilepsy for which a tertiary specialist may consider a ketogenic diet.

Activities of daily living

Activities of daily living
Explore effects on lifestyle and social activities, including experiences of exclusion.
Activities of daily living
Discuss driving and Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency (DVLA) rules.
Activities of daily living

Carers

Medication

Mental health

artifacts.description: Topics offered for discussion at each appointment with the person with epilepsy and, when appropriate, their family or carers. The accompanying guidance also directs clinicians to safety considerations and Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) advice on antiepileptic drugs in pregnancy, valproate and topiramate.
artifacts.summary: This checklist organises discussions about everyday safety, carers, cognition, medication, mental health, reproductive health and SUDEP. It helps ensure that concerns relevant to the person and their family or carers can be raised during appointments.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: These topics support shared decisions, safer daily activities, medication adherence and discussion of reproductive and epilepsy-related mortality risks.

Do not initiate sodium valproate unless 2 specialists independently agree and record that no other effective and tolerated treatment exists, or that compelling reasons mean the reproductive risks do not apply.
Women and girls of childbearing potential, including girls likely to require treatment when old enough to have children
Use sodium valproate only if other treatment options have been unsuccessful.
Women and girls of childbearing potential, including girls likely to require treatment when old enough to have children
Fully discuss benefits and risks, including risks to an unborn child.
Women and girls of childbearing potential, including girls likely to require treatment when old enough to have children
Consider the likelihood of pregnancy and establish the Pregnancy Prevention Programme if appropriate.
Boys and men

artifacts.description: The measures distinguish restrictions on first-time prescribing, conditions for use in women and girls of childbearing potential, and contraceptive and fertility advice for boys and men.
artifacts.summary: This checklist sets out MHRA restrictions and precautions for sodium valproate according to age and reproductive circumstances. It informs prescribing and counselling when sodium valproate is considered.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: It identifies conditions that must be addressed before initiating or using sodium valproate and the reproductive precautions to discuss during treatment.

special_populations.population: Children and young people with epilepsy
special_populations.considerations: Include them in discussions using information suited to their developmental age. Agree individually tailored monitoring reviews at least every 12 months. Provide access to an epilepsy specialist nurse and plan the transition to adult services around the young person's needs.

special_populations.population: Children under 3 years with suspected or confirmed epilepsy
special_populations.considerations: Arrange assessment by a tertiary paediatric epilepsy service within 2 weeks because epilepsy beginning at this age can be associated with developmental difficulties.

special_populations.population: Children under 4 years with myoclonic seizures
special_populations.considerations: Seek treatment advice from, or refer the child to, a tertiary paediatric neurologist. Onset at this age may indicate an underlying neurodegenerative disorder.

special_populations.population: Children under 2 years with suspected or confirmed infantile spasms
special_populations.considerations: Within 24 hours, obtain guidance from and urgently refer to a tertiary paediatric neurologist. Assessment should include sleep EEG. Review at least weekly during treatment, repeat sleep EEG at 2 weeks after treatment starts, and review monthly once spasms stop.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: For spasms not caused by tuberous sclerosis, offer high-dose oral prednisolone with vigabatrin as first-line treatment unless steroid-related adverse effects pose a high risk; in that case, consider vigabatrin alone. For spasms due to tuberous sclerosis, offer vigabatrin alone and add high-dose oral prednisolone if it is ineffective after 1 week.

special_populations.population: Children and young people with self-limited epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes
special_populations.considerations: Discuss whether to start medication in light of seizure frequency and severity, the hazards of continuing seizures and treatment adverse effects. If school performance deteriorates, seek specialist advice and consider sleep EEG and neuropsychology assessment; consider sleep EEG if other seizure types develop. Tailor follow-up to individual needs.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Discuss stopping treatment after at least 2 years without seizures or at age 14 years.

special_populations.considerations: Account for comorbidities, possible interactions with other medicines and the need for accessible information or additional time and support during appointments.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Individualise antiseizure medication dosing and titration, usually beginning at a lower dose and increasing it slowly.

special_populations.population: People with epilepsy and a learning disability, physical disability, mental health problem or other complex needs
special_populations.considerations: Adapt communication and support to individual needs. People with a learning disability, physical disability or mental health problem may need help accessing tertiary epilepsy services. Coordinate care across relevant teams when a mental health condition or learning disability is present. Do not exclude a person with a learning disability from referral for resective epilepsy surgery assessment when it is indicated.

special_populations.population: People with epilepsy and underlying genetic abnormalities
special_populations.considerations: An underlying genetic abnormality must not prevent referral for resective epilepsy surgery assessment when that assessment is indicated.

special_populations.population: People of Han Chinese or Thai family background
special_populations.considerations: phenytoin is associated with an increased risk of serious skin reactions. carbamazepine and potentially structurally similar medicines, including oxcarbazepine and eslicarbazepine acetate, are also associated with increased risk of serious skin reactions.

special_populations.population: People of European or Japanese family background
special_populations.considerations: carbamazepine and potentially structurally similar medicines, including oxcarbazepine and eslicarbazepine acetate, are associated with an increased risk of serious skin reactions.
The restriction on starting sodium valproate applies to both males and females because of reproductive risks.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Do not start sodium valproate for the first time unless 2 specialists independently agree and document that no other effective and tolerated treatment exists, or that compelling reasons mean the reproductive risks do not apply.

special_populations.population: Women and girls of childbearing potential
special_populations.considerations: Regularly revisit age-appropriate information about contraception, folic acid supplementation, conception, pregnancy, breastfeeding, childcare and menopause. Discuss potential fetal risks from antiseizure medications, including congenital malformations, neurodevelopmental impairment and restricted fetal growth. Some antiseizure medications can reduce hormonal contraceptive effectiveness, while oestrogen-containing hormonal contraception can reduce the effectiveness of lamotrigine.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Do not use sodium valproate or topiramate unless the conditions of the Pregnancy Prevention Programme are fulfilled. Use sodium valproate only when other treatment options are unsuccessful, risks and benefits have been fully discussed, and the likelihood of pregnancy has been considered.

special_populations.considerations: Explain the possible association between paternal sodium valproate use around conception and neurodevelopmental disorders in children; a causal role is unknown. Discuss potential fertility risks and treatment options with men planning a family within the next year.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Advise effective contraception consisting of condoms plus contraception used by a female sexual partner throughout valproate treatment and for 3 months after stopping. Refer men taking sodium valproate who plan a family within the next year to an epilepsy specialist team to review medication options.

special_populations.population: Women and girls with epilepsy who are planning pregnancy
special_populations.considerations: Refer to an epilepsy specialist team to review medication options. Discuss the balance between risks from poorly controlled seizures and risks to the baby from antiseizure medication during pregnancy or breastfeeding. Consider monitoring medication levels when seizure worsening is a concern.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: When medication-level monitoring begins, obtain a pre-conception baseline concentration for medicines such as carbamazepine, lamotrigine, levetiracetam, oxcarbazepine, phenobarbital and phenytoin, and check adherence.

special_populations.population: Women and girls with epilepsy who are pregnant
special_populations.considerations: Arrange an epilepsy specialist review and share care information with specialist obstetric and primary care teams. Emphasise adherence and advise against stopping antiseizure medication without medical supervision. Consider more frequent reviews for those with a learning disability, aged under 16 years, with a seizure within the past 12 months, with bilateral tonic-clonic seizures or with modifiable SUDEP risk factors.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: For those taking carbamazepine, lamotrigine, levetiracetam, oxcarbazepine, phenobarbital or phenytoin, monitor and adjust doses according to MHRA pregnancy safety advice. If doses change during pregnancy, agree an antenatal plan to begin returning to preconception doses in the first few days after birth.

special_populations.population: Women and girls with epilepsy who are breastfeeding
special_populations.considerations: Explain that breastfeeding while taking most antiseizure medications is generally safe for the baby and should be encouraged. Support an individual feeding choice after considering breastfeeding benefits and possible medication effects on the child.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Consult the individual medicine advice in the SPC and the BNF or BNF for children when prescribing antiseizure medication.

special_populations.population: Young people with complex or additional health and social care needs transitioning to adult epilepsy services
special_populations.considerations: Begin transition planning early, particularly when seizures remain uncontrolled or the young person has a learning disability. Paediatric and adult multidisciplinary teams should jointly review the diagnosis and management plan with the young person and, when appropriate, their family or carers. Share accessible information and revisit it during transition.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Children, young people and adults with confirmed epilepsy; treatment may also be considered after a first unprovoked seizure in specified circumstances.
decision_rules: Agree an individualised medication strategy that accounts for seizure type, epilepsy syndrome, whether treatment is needed, other medicines and conditions, reproductive plans, personal circumstances and the person's preferences.
Start an antiseizure medication when epilepsy is confirmed.

After a first unprovoked seizure, consider starting treatment if examination shows neurological deficit, EEG shows unequivocal epileptic activity, imaging shows a structural abnormality, or the person or their family or carers find the risk of further seizures unacceptable.
Use monotherapy whenever possible. If seizures persist at an optimal first-line dose, reconsider the epilepsy diagnosis. If the diagnosis remains confirmed, try a different monotherapy.

When changing monotherapy, slowly increase the new medicine while maintaining the first; if the new treatment works, gradually withdraw the first. If it fails, gradually withdraw the new medicine and consider another option.

If monotherapy fails, consider an add-on medicine, titrate it carefully and review treatment and adverse effects frequently. If add-on trials do not reduce seizures, use the regimen with the best balance of effectiveness and tolerability.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Discuss the value of using as few medicines as possible to maintain seizure freedom or control. For older people, check interactions and individualise dosing and titration, usually beginning at a lower dose and increasing slowly. Apply the MHRA restrictions on sodium valproate and topiramate where relevant.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: People with epilepsy considering withdrawal of antiseizure medication, particularly after being seizure-free for 2 years.
decision_rules: Discuss the potential benefits and risks of stopping treatment during ongoing reviews.
After 2 years without seizures, assess individual recurrence risk; involve an epilepsy specialist if the risks cause doubt or concern.
Account for recurrence and, where appropriate, SUDEP risk, as well as preferences, lifestyle and driving implications.
If stopping treatment is agreed, plan a gradual reduction. Withdraw multiple medicines one at a time.
If seizures return during or after withdrawal, reverse the last dose reduction and obtain epilepsy specialist guidance.
After epilepsy surgery, withdraw antiseizure medicines only with guidance from the epilepsy surgery centre.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: For most medicines, tapering would typically take at least 3 months; benzodiazepines and barbiturates would typically require a longer period to reduce withdrawal symptoms.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: People with generalised tonic-clonic seizures receiving monotherapy.
decision_rules: Offer a choice of the listed first-line monotherapies. If the initial choice fails, try another listed medicine, followed by the third if needed.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Children, young people and adults having a convulsive seizure lasting 5 minutes or more.
decision_rules: Provide resuscitation and immediate emergency treatment.
If an individualised emergency management plan is immediately available, give the medicine it specifies.
Otherwise, immediately give buccal midazolam or rectal diazepam in the community; use intravenous lorazepam if intravenous access and resuscitation facilities are immediately available.

If the first benzodiazepine dose fails, call emergency services in the community or seek expert hospital guidance. Follow an immediately available individualised plan, or give a second benzodiazepine dose if the seizure has not stopped within 5 to 10 minutes of the first.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: People with certain childhood-onset epilepsy syndromes or drug-resistant epilepsy when other treatments have failed or are unsuitable.
decision_rules: Consider a ketogenic diet under a tertiary epilepsy specialist rather than using it routinely. Childhood-onset examples include glucose transporter type 1 deficiency syndrome (GLUT1 deficiency syndrome), epilepsy associated with pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency, infantile spasms syndrome, epilepsy with myoclonic-atonic seizures (Doose syndrome), Dravet syndrome and Lennox–Gastaut syndrome.
