Refer women and girls planning pregnancy or pregnant for specialist review of antiseizure options, and share pregnancy-care information among epilepsy specialists, specialist obstetrics and primary care. Explain the importance of adherence and not stopping medication without supervision. Discuss the relative maternal seizure-control and infant medication-exposure risks when considering changes before pregnancy or during breastfeeding. Consider more frequent reviews during pregnancy for those taking antiseizure medication who have learning disability, are under 16 years, had a seizure within the past 12 months, have bilateral tonic-clonic seizures or have modifiable SUDEP risks. Consider drug-level monitoring before pregnancy if worsening seizures are a concern. When beginning such monitoring, establish a pre-conception drug concentration and assess adherence; examples include carbamazepine, lamotrigine, levetiracetam, oxcarbazepine, phenobarbital and phenytoin. During pregnancy or pregnancy planning with these medicines, monitor and adjust doses in accordance with MHRA advice. Discuss pregnancy monitoring results and dose choices. If pregnancy required dose changes, make an antenatal plan to begin returning to preconception doses during the first few days after birth.

document_sections.heading: 4.6 Discontinuing antiseizure medication
document_sections.content: At any review, discuss withdrawal benefits and risks using accessible information. After 2 years without seizures, assess individual recurrence risk if treatment stops, involving an epilepsy specialist if risks are uncertain or concerning. Discuss recurrence and, where relevant, SUDEP risk, preferences, lifestyle and driving. If withdrawal is agreed, make an individual plan for gradual reduction, typically over at least 3 months for most medicines and longer for benzodiazepines and barbiturates. Stop multiple medicines one at a time. If seizures return during or after withdrawal, reverse the most recent reduction and seek specialist advice according to the plan. Withdrawal after epilepsy surgery should be guided by its surgery centre.

document_sections.heading: Box 2 MHRA safety measures and precautionary advice for sodium valproate
document_sections.content: Do not initiate sodium valproate in a person younger than 55 years unless 2 specialists independently agree and record that no effective, tolerated alternative exists or compelling reasons render reproductive risks inapplicable. For women and girls who could become pregnant, use it only after other treatments have failed, full discussion of benefits and risks including fetal harm, and assessment of pregnancy likelihood with the Pregnancy Prevention Programme where appropriate. Advise boys and men to use condoms alongside contraception used by a female sexual partner throughout treatment and for 3 months after stopping; advise men planning a family within the next year about possible fertility risks and alternatives.

document_sections.heading: 5.1 Generalised tonic-clonic seizures
document_sections.content: Offer lamotrigine, levetiracetam or sodium valproate as first-line monotherapy, trying the remaining choices sequentially if treatment fails; observe box 2 for sodium valproate. If monotherapy fails, consider first-line add-on clobazam, lamotrigine, levetiracetam, perampanel, sodium valproate or topiramate, trying other listed options if needed. If those fail, consider second-line add-on brivaracetam, lacosamide, phenobarbital, primidone or zonisamide, moving among them if unsuccessful. Do not use topiramate for women or girls who could become pregnant without meeting Pregnancy Prevention Programme conditions. carbamazepine, gabapentin, oxcarbazepine, phenytoin, pregabalin, tiagabine and vigabatrin may worsen coexisting absence or myoclonic seizures, including juvenile myoclonic epilepsy; lamotrigine may worsen myoclonic seizures. In January 2025, specified uses were off-label: lamotrigine in children under 13 years and levetiracetam in adults and children as monotherapy; some add-on medicines in children; brivaracetam in adults and children, lacosamide in children under 4 years, and zonisamide in adults and children as second-line add-ons.

document_sections.heading: 5.2 Focal seizures with or without evolution to bilateral tonic-clonic seizures
document_sections.content: Consider lamotrigine or levetiracetam first as monotherapy and switch to the other if needed. If both fail, consider second-line monotherapy with carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine or zonisamide, trying other listed choices after failure; then consider lacosamide as third-line monotherapy. If monotherapy fails, consider first-line add-on carbamazepine, lacosamide, lamotrigine, levetiracetam, oxcarbazepine, topiramate or zonisamide, trying the other options if necessary. After first-line add-ons fail, consider brivaracetam, cenobamate under TA753, 2025, eslicarbazepine acetate, perampanel or pregabalin as second-line add-ons. After these fail, consider third-line add-on phenobarbital, phenytoin, sodium valproate, tiagabine or vigabatrin. Follow box 2 for sodium valproate and require Pregnancy Prevention Programme conditions for topiramate in women and girls who could become pregnant. In January 2025, listed off-label uses included lamotrigine below 13 years; levetiracetam below 16 years; oxcarbazepine below 6 years; zonisamide in children; lacosamide below 2 years; some add-on medicines in children; and tiagabine below 12 years.

document_sections.heading: 5.3 Absence seizures
document_sections.content: For absence seizures, including childhood absence epilepsy, offer ethosuximide first. If unsuccessful, offer lamotrigine, levetiracetam or sodium valproate as second-line monotherapy or add-on treatment, trying the remaining options sequentially and observing box 2. carbamazepine, gabapentin, oxcarbazepine, phenobarbital, phenytoin, pregabalin, tiagabine and vigabatrin may worsen absence seizures. For absence seizures alongside other seizure types, or risk of them, consider lamotrigine, levetiracetam or sodium valproate first, as monotherapy or add-on therapy, trying the other options if needed. If these fail, consider ethosuximide only as a second-line add-on. The same listed medicines may aggravate seizures in this group. In January 2025, specified uses of lamotrigine below 2 years and levetiracetam in adults and children, and some medicines for combined seizure types in children, were off-label.

document_sections.heading: 5.4 Myoclonic seizures
document_sections.content: For a child under 4 years, seek treatment advice from or refer to a tertiary paediatric neurologist. Offer levetiracetam or sodium valproate first and try the other as monotherapy or add-on if necessary, observing box 2. If unsuccessful, consider brivaracetam, clobazam, clonazepam, lamotrigine, phenobarbital, piracetam, topiramate or zonisamide alone or as an add-on, moving to other listed options as needed. lamotrigine can occasionally worsen myoclonic seizures. Do not use carbamazepine, gabapentin, oxcarbazepine, phenytoin, pregabalin, tiagabine or vigabatrin because they may aggravate seizures. Require Pregnancy Prevention Programme conditions before topiramate in women and girls who could become pregnant. In January 2025, levetiracetam monotherapy and some second-line uses in children were off-label.

document_sections.heading: 5.5 Tonic or atonic seizures
document_sections.content: Arrange assessment by an epilepsy-experienced neurologist for syndrome diagnosis where possible and advice on investigations and care. Offer lamotrigine or sodium valproate first, trying the other alone or as an add-on if needed; follow box 2. If unsuccessful, consider clobazam, rufinamide or topiramate alone or as an add-on and try remaining choices if needed. Topiramate requires Pregnancy Prevention Programme conditions for those who could become pregnant. If second-line treatment fails in children, consider add-on ketogenic diet supervised by its specialist team. If every other option fails, consider add-on felbamate under an epilepsy-experienced neurologist. carbamazepine, gabapentin, oxcarbazepine, pregabalin, tiagabine and vigabatrin may worsen these seizures. In January 2025, specified lamotrigine use below 13 years as monotherapy and below 2 years as add-on, and some second-line uses, were off-label; felbamate was not licensed in the UK.

document_sections.heading: 5.6 Idiopathic generalised epilepsies
document_sections.content: Offer lamotrigine, levetiracetam or sodium valproate first, trying the remaining options as monotherapy or add-ons if needed and following box 2. If first-line choices fail, consider perampanel or topiramate as second-line add-ons, trying the other if necessary. Do not use topiramate in women or girls who could become pregnant unless Pregnancy Prevention Programme conditions are met. In January 2025, lamotrigine monotherapy below 13 years, add-on below 2 years and levetiracetam monotherapy in adults and children were off-label, as were perampanel below 7 years and topiramate below 2 years.

document_sections.heading: 6.1 Dravet syndrome
document_sections.content: Involve an adult or paediatric neurologist experienced in epilepsy. Consider sodium valproate first despite the need for caution, because syndrome severity and lack of evidence for effective alternative first-line therapy justify its recommendation; follow box 2. If sodium valproate alone fails, consider adding stiripentol and clobazam as first-line triple therapy, titrating cautiously and reviewing frequently for effects such as sedation. For a child aged 2 years or over whose triple therapy fails, consider second-line add-on fenfluramine under TA808, 2022, or cannabidiol with clobazam under TA614, 2019, following their stopping criteria. For children under 2 years after triple-therapy failure, or those aged 2 years or over after second-line failure, consider ketogenic diet, levetiracetam or topiramate as add-ons under appropriate specialist supervision; try other listed choices if necessary. If all options fail, consider potassium bromide under specialist guidance. carbamazepine, gabapentin, lacosamide, lamotrigine, oxcarbazepine, phenobarbital, pregabalin, tiagabine and vigabatrin may aggravate seizures. Apply Pregnancy Prevention Programme restrictions to topiramate. In April 2022, clobazam add-on below 6 months and stiripentol initiation above 18 years were off-label; in January 2025, levetiracetam and topiramate uses were off-label and potassium bromide was unlicensed in the UK.

document_sections.heading: 6.2 Lennox–Gastaut syndrome
document_sections.content: Involve an adult or paediatric neurologist experienced in epilepsy. Consider sodium valproate first with caution and box 2 safeguards: the syndrome is severe and evidence for other effective first-line choices is lacking. If it fails, consider lamotrigine alone or as an add-on. If second-line therapy fails, consider third-line add-on cannabidiol with clobazam for children aged 2 years or over under TA615, 2019; clobazam; fenfluramine for children aged 2 years or over under TA1050, 2025; rufinamide; or topiramate. Follow relevant technology appraisal stopping guidance and Pregnancy Prevention Programme restrictions. Titrate add-ons carefully and review frequently for sedation and other adverse effects. If seizures persist, consider supervised add-on ketogenic diet; if every other option fails, consider specialist-supervised add-on felbamate. carbamazepine, gabapentin, lacosamide, lamotrigine, oxcarbazepine, phenobarbital, pregabalin, tiagabine and vigabatrin may exacerbate seizures, despite lamotrigine's second-line role. In January 2025, lamotrigine monotherapy below 13 years and add-on below 2 years, clobazam add-on below 6 months, rufinamide below 1 year and topiramate below 2 years were off-label. In April 2022, felbamate was unlicensed in the UK.

document_sections.heading: 6.3 Infantile spasms syndrome
document_sections.content: For suspected or confirmed spasms in a child under 2 years, obtain tertiary paediatric neurology guidance and urgently refer within 24 hours for rapid assessment, including sleep EEG, and treatment. Review at least weekly during therapy and repeat sleep EEG at 2 weeks; after spasms cease, review monthly and repeat sleep EEG for recurrence or clinical concern. For spasms unrelated to tuberous sclerosis, offer high-dose oral prednisolone plus vigabatrin first unless steroid adverse-effect risk is high; then consider vigabatrin alone. For spasms due to tuberous sclerosis, offer vigabatrin alone first and add high-dose oral prednisolone if ineffective after 1 week. Before prednisolone, discuss steroid harms, test varicella zoster virus antibodies and give parents or carers a steroid card and advice on seeking help. Follow BNF for children prednisolone doses and check blood pressure and urinary glucose weekly. Increase vigabatrin according to BNF for children and discuss additional escalation with tertiary paediatric neurology if clinical spasms and EEG abnormalities persist. If first-line therapy fails, discuss care with a tertiary paediatric epilepsy specialist and consider supervised ketogenic diet, levetiracetam, nitrazepam, sodium valproate or topiramate as second-line monotherapy or add-on; consider other listed choices if one fails. In January 2025, combining vigabatrin with prednisolone and second-line levetiracetam, nitrazepam and topiramate were off-label; the combination was also identified as off-label in April 2022.

document_sections.heading: 6.4 Self-limited epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes
document_sections.content: Discuss with children, young people and their families whether to treat, considering seizure frequency and severity, ongoing-seizure hazards including a small death risk, and treatment harms. Consider lamotrigine or levetiracetam first and try the other if needed. If both fail, consider second-line monotherapy carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine or zonisamide, moving among them if necessary. If unsuccessful, consider sulthiame alone or as an add-on only after discussion with a tertiary paediatric neurologist. carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine and lamotrigine may rarely worsen seizures, contribute to another epilepsy syndrome or impair cognition in a small number of children and young people. For concerning school performance during treatment, consult an epilepsy specialist and consider sleep EEG to exclude electrical status epilepticus during sleep and neuropsychological assessment. For new seizure types during treatment, consider sleep EEG to exclude developmental epileptic encephalopathy with spike-wave activation in sleep. Tailor follow-up and discuss stopping treatment after at least 2 years without seizures or at age 14 years. In January 2025, lamotrigine below 13 years, levetiracetam below 16 years, oxcarbazepine below 6 years and zonisamide in adults and children were specified as off-label. An update dated November 2025 states that sulthiame is now licensed in the UK and recommendations 6.4.2 to 6.4.4 are under review.

document_sections.heading: 6.5 Epilepsy with myoclonic-atonic seizures (Doose syndrome)
document_sections.content: Discuss children's care with a tertiary paediatric neurologist. Consider levetiracetam or sodium valproate first, trying the other if necessary and applying box 2. If these fail, consider supervised ketogenic diet alone or as an add-on. If it fails, consider clobazam, ethosuximide, topiramate or zonisamide as third-line monotherapy or add-on, trying other listed options after failure. Require Pregnancy Prevention Programme conditions for topiramate in women and girls who could become pregnant. Do not use carbamazepine, gabapentin, oxcarbazepine, phenytoin, pregabalin or vigabatrin because seizures may worsen. Consider stopping antiseizure treatment in children seizure-free for 2 years. In January 2025, levetiracetam, clobazam monotherapy in adults and children or add-on below 6 months, and topiramate and zonisamide in adults and children were specified as off-label.

document_sections.heading: 6.6 Treatments for other childhood-onset seizures
document_sections.content: NICE technology appraisal guidance recommends cannabidiol as an add-on option for some children aged 2 years and over with seizures due to tuberous sclerosis complex; TA873, 2023 supplies eligibility and stopping details. NICE technology appraisal guidance does not recommend add-on ganaxolone for seizures due to cyclin-dependent kinase-like 5 (CDKL5) deficiency disorder in children aged 2 years and over; see TA1033, 2025.

document_sections.heading: 7.1 Status epilepticus
document_sections.content: Convulsive status epilepticus means seizures lasting 5 minutes or more; provide immediate emergency treatment and resuscitation. Follow an immediately available individual emergency plan. Otherwise, immediately give buccal midazolam or rectal diazepam in the community, or intravenous lorazepam when intravenous access and resuscitation are immediately available. Consider causes including hypoglycaemia, eclampsia, alcohol withdrawal and non-adherence, and recognise that dissociative seizures can resemble convulsive status epilepticus. After failure of the first benzodiazepine dose, call emergency services in the community or obtain expert hospital advice. Continue an available emergency plan or give a second benzodiazepine dose if the seizure persists 5 to 10 minutes after the first. After 2 unsuccessful doses, give intravenous levetiracetam, phenytoin or sodium valproate as second-line treatment, following box 2 for sodium valproate; levetiracetam may be faster to administer and cause fewer adverse effects. Under expert guidance, consider another second-line option if necessary, then phenobarbital or general anaesthesia if second-line choices fail. Afterward, agree an emergency plan when none exists and recurrence is a concern. Intravenous levetiracetam was off-label in April 2022.

document_sections.heading: 7.2 Repeated seizures or cluster seizures
document_sections.content: Treat clusters, typically 3 or more seizures that stop by themselves within 24 hours, as an emergency. Follow an immediately available individual plan; otherwise consider immediate benzodiazepine such as clobazam or midazolam. Obtain expert advice if clusters recur, and agree a personal emergency plan if recurrence is a concern and none exists.

document_sections.heading: 7.3 Prolonged seizures
document_sections.content: Treat a convulsive seizure lasting more than 2 minutes beyond the person's usual seizure duration as an emergency; at 5 minutes or more, use status epilepticus recommendations. Follow an available individual plan or consider immediate midazolam or clobazam if no plan is immediately available. Following a prolonged convulsive seizure, agree an emergency plan if recurrence is a concern and no plan exists. Do the same following a non-convulsive seizure lasting more than 2 minutes beyond its usual duration.

document_sections.heading: 8.1 Ketogenic diet
document_sections.content: Consider ketogenic diet under tertiary epilepsy specialist guidance for certain childhood-onset conditions, including glucose transporter type 1 deficiency syndrome (GLUT1 deficiency syndrome), epilepsy associated with pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency, infantile spasms syndrome, epilepsy with myoclonic-atonic seizures (Doose syndrome), Dravet syndrome and Lennox–Gastaut syndrome. Also consider it for drug-resistant epilepsy when other treatments fail or are inappropriate.

document_sections.heading: 8.2 Resective epilepsy surgery
document_sections.content: Discuss assessment for resective surgery with people with drug-resistant epilepsy, explaining assessment procedures, potential benefits and harms. Refer adults to tertiary epilepsy services and children or young people to tertiary paediatric neurology services for consideration of a children's epilepsy surgery centre, even when MRI shows no abnormality. Consider early tertiary referral and possible surgical assessment when MRI lesions suggest high drug-resistance risk, including hippocampal sclerosis, cortical-development malformations, epilepsy-associated low-grade tumours, hypothalamic hamartomas, neuronal migrational disorders, tuberous sclerosis complex, vascular malformations including Sturge–Weber syndrome, and cerebral contusions from previous injury. Do not exclude indicated surgical referrals because of learning disability or genetic abnormalities.

document_sections.heading: 8.3 Vagus nerve stimulation
document_sections.content: If resective surgery is unsuitable for drug-resistant seizures, consider vagus nerve stimulation in addition to antiseizure medication. Discuss its benefits and harms with the person and, where appropriate, family or carers before deciding jointly.

document_sections.heading: 9.1 Providing coordinated care
document_sections.content: Compared with the general population, people with epilepsy more often have mental health difficulties, learning disabilities, neurodevelopmental conditions including attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and autism spectrum disorder, or dementia, and face greater suicide risk. Coordinate care through a multidisciplinary team for coexisting mental health conditions or learning disability. Complex childhood epilepsy can entail developmental and cognitive difficulties requiring additional multidisciplinary support. Ensure communication among relevant services and apply the referenced NICE recommendations for coordinating care in learning disability, challenging behaviour, mental health problems or dementia.

document_sections.heading: 9.2 Support and treatment
document_sections.content: Recognise that an epilepsy diagnosis may substantially affect mental health and be accompanied by exclusion or stigma. Routinely review development, cognition, mental health, emotional and social wellbeing, and learning disabilities. Assess depression and offer support and treatment according to the cited NICE depression guidelines. Remain alert to anxiety, other mental health problems and suicide risk; if concerns arise, consider referral and follow applicable NICE guidance for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, autism spectrum disorder, learning-disability-related mental health difficulties, anxiety, panic disorder, psychosis and schizophrenia.

document_sections.heading: 10.1 Risk factors
document_sections.content: Epilepsy carries increased premature-death risk, including SUDEP. Potentially modifiable SUDEP risks include medication non-adherence, alcohol or drug misuse, focal to bilateral tonic-clonic or generalised tonic-clonic seizures, uncontrolled seizures, living alone and sleeping without supervision. Prior brain injury, central nervous system infection, metastatic cancer, stroke and abnormal neurological examination findings raise epilepsy-related death risk. From diagnosis onward, discuss each person's individual death and SUDEP risk with them and, where appropriate, family or carers; for young children, discuss it with parents or carers. Agree possible risk-reduction measures. For sleep-related seizures, specifically discuss SUDEP and ways to minimise risk, including taking medication as prescribed.

document_sections.heading: 10.2 Interventions
document_sections.content: For someone with nocturnal seizures assessed as having higher epilepsy-related death risk, discuss starting or increasing night-time supervision, potentially using a night monitor. Support prescribed medication use to reduce seizures, explaining that uncontrolled seizures increase death risk, particularly with generalised tonic-clonic or focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizures.

document_sections.heading: 11.1 Epilepsy specialist nurses
document_sections.content: Ensure access to an epilepsy specialist nurse for every child, young person and adult with epilepsy. This nurse should provide information, education and support, assist professionals across healthcare, education, respite and social care, and facilitate community and multiagency access. Offer an individual information and care-planning session that addresses emotional wellbeing and self-management supporting participation and inclusion. When seizures continue, offer nurse sessions at least twice a year and after A&E visits. Consider nurse-led educational groups for young people and adults.

document_sections.heading: 11.2 Transition from children's to adults' epilepsy services
document_sections.content: Involve young people in individually tailored transition planning. Begin early when seizures remain uncontrolled or additional health or social needs, including learning disability, complicate transition. Paediatric and adult multidisciplinary teams should jointly review diagnosis and management with the young person and, where appropriate, family or carers. Discuss and share an accessible transition and care plan in understandable language, repeating information at different times. Address daily living, driving, sport, adherence, mood, memory, education or work, independent living, development, cognition, behaviour, alcohol and illicit drugs, safety and SUDEP, contraception, pregnancy, teratogenicity, sleep, disclosure, social assumptions and stigma.

document_sections.heading: Terms used in this guideline
document_sections.content: The guideline's seizure and syndrome terminology draws on the International League Against Epilepsy's proposed classification framework.

document_sections.heading: Drug-resistant epilepsy
document_sections.content: This denotes persistent seizures with sustained seizure freedom very unlikely through further antiseizure medication changes. The International League Against Epilepsy definition requires failure of adequate trials of 2 tolerated, appropriately selected and used medication schedules, given alone or together, to achieve sustained seizure freedom.

document_sections.heading: MRI protocols
document_sections.content: An epilepsy MRI protocol combines brain-imaging sequences to improve detection of structural abnormalities that may cause epilepsy. A regionally agreed standard aims for consistent, high-quality diagnosis.

document_sections.heading: Suboptimal MRI
document_sections.content: MRI is suboptimal when its sequence set is inadequate or inappropriate, or image quality is poor, for example because of movement.

document_sections.heading: Tertiary epilepsy service
document_sections.content: This specialist adult or paediatric neurology service investigates and manages complex epilepsy. It offers neuropsychology, neuropsychiatry, specialised imaging including 3T MRI, and specialised neurophysiology including video EEG telemetry. It can assess people with learning disabilities, pregnant women, people moving between services and older people, and provide access to specialised nonsurgical care, genetic diagnosis and counselling, surgical assessment, vagus nerve stimulation and research.

document_sections.heading: Unprovoked seizure
document_sections.content: A seizure without an immediate precipitating event such as fever, head injury, alcohol or drug consumption.

document_sections.heading: Unsuccessful treatment
document_sections.content: Treatment is unsuccessful when seizures do not diminish or cease, or adverse effects are intolerable to the person.

document_sections.heading: Key recommendations for research
document_sections.content: The committee proposes research into effective immunomodulation for defined autoimmune epilepsy syndromes; treatment after unsuccessful or intolerable first-line therapy for Dravet syndrome, Lennox–Gastaut syndrome, infantile spasms syndrome and epilepsy with myoclonic-atonic seizures (Doose syndrome); development and external validation of a tool predicting all-cause epilepsy-related death including SUDEP; vagus nerve stimulation effectiveness, including in people with learning disabilities; and the cost effectiveness of tailored psychological treatment.

document_sections.heading: Other recommendations for research
document_sections.content: Further proposed studies concern clinical and cost effectiveness of antiseizure-drug level monitoring for girls and women, digital health technologies, antiseizure medicines for seizure clusters, and short- and long-term ketogenic-diet effectiveness, cost and tolerability in drug-resistant epilepsy. The committee also proposes developing and externally validating a tool predicting a second seizure after a single seizure.

document_sections.heading: Referral after a first seizure or remission and assessing risk of a second seizure
document_sections.content: The committee considered rapid specialist referral important because epilepsy diagnosis is complex and errors can lead to inappropriate care. Evidence suggested adults with a mental health condition after a first seizure were almost 3 times more likely to have another seizure than the general population; those with sepsis were 4.5 times more likely than those without sepsis. Vascular-risk evidence did not show a risk difference, but the committee regarded diabetes, hypertension and atrial fibrillation as important potentially modifiable factors. Evidence about children's temperature and recurrence risk was unclear: febrile seizures generally do not predispose to later afebrile seizures, whereas afebrile seizures may increase recurrence risk. Individual risk assessment therefore also needs mental, physical and social factors. The committee did not recommend existing second-seizure prediction tools because poor discrimination between low and high risk could cause harm. Only about 25% of adults currently receive complete modifiable-risk assessment after a first seizure; changing this may modestly increase staff costs. The recommendations for children reflect existing practice.

document_sections.heading: Specialist assessment and diagnosis
document_sections.content:
The committee set maximum acceptable false-negative and false-positive rates at 10% each, corresponding to minimum sensitivity and specificity of 0.9; most reviewed tests did not meet these thresholds. Specialist history and examination surpassed them in adult evidence, which the committee considered applicable to younger people. Witness reports and recordings can improve expert assessment but lacked sufficient accuracy independently. ECG helps identify cardiac mimics, and metabolic assessment can identify alternative causes. Imaging investigates structural causes rather than diagnosing epilepsy alone. Routine interictal EEG has low sensitivity, so a normal result cannot exclude epilepsy; its specificity allows a positive finding to support a provisional clinical diagnosis. Earlier EEG, ideally within 72 hours, may improve accuracy. Provoking manoeuvres and sleep or ambulatory recordings over 48 hours may slightly increase sensitivity but still cannot exclude epilepsy when negative; discuss their possible harms and benefits. Ambulatory EEG may be particularly useful when focal epilepsy is suspected. The recommendations are not expected to substantially change practice.

The recommendations are not expected to alter practice substantially.

document_sections.heading: Neuroimaging
document_sections.content: Imaging can identify an epilepsy cause, inform prognosis and guide management. The committee considered it unnecessary when structural brain abnormalities are not expected, as in idiopathic generalised epilepsy and self-limited epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes. MRI was preferred, although the evidence did not assess competing MRI protocols. Regionally agreed epilepsy protocols should provide adequate detail using sequences available on most modern scanners. MRI should occur no later than 6 weeks after referral to support timely decisions and align with the Handbook to the NHS Constitution for England. CT can substitute when MRI is unsuitable, such as with severe claustrophobia or a nonMRI conditional pacemaker. Interpretation depends on radiological expertise; specialist tertiary review may be appropriate when diagnosis is uncertain or epilepsy is drug resistant. Repeat MRI may clarify new symptoms, changes in lesions or seizure-generating areas before surgery. CT can investigate an acute lesion or illness after a new-onset acute symptomatic seizure, but is unnecessary after a typical seizure in someone with established epilepsy unless other concerns exist. Imaging use currently varies; these recommendations may increase scanning while standardised protocols may reduce later repeat scans.

document_sections.heading: Genetic testing
document_sections.content: A neurologist or geneticist can help resolve uncertainty about whom to test and which test to use. Access varies and may expand. The NHS National Genomic Test Directory for rare and inherited disease identifies epilepsy tests commissioned nationally by the NHS in England and their indications. A genetic diagnosis may guide treatment, prognosis, assessment of related conditions and family counselling, but results can have emotional and social implications for relatives as well as the person tested. Before testing, discuss its purpose, benefits, limitations, risks, possible results and appropriate sharing of information; document informed consent and provide genetic counselling. Evidence did not justify testing everyone with epilepsy or establish a particular point in the care pathway for testing. The committee targeted whole-genome sequencing toward epilepsy beginning under 2 years or accompanied by developmental disorders or suggestive clinical features, consistent with clinical indication R59. For unexplained epilepsy beginning between 2 and 3 years, diagnostic yield depends partly on co-occurring conditions and MRI and EEG findings; whole-genome sequencing should be considered when agreed by a specialist multidisciplinary team. Testing is not routinely performed even when a genetic cause is suspected. Clarifying eligibility may increase genetic tests and counselling referrals but may reduce uninformative testing.

document_sections.heading: Antibody testing
document_sections.content: Limited evidence did not support routine antibody testing in epilepsy. The committee considered testing when autoimmune encephalitis is suspected in new-onset epilepsy: this condition can cause seizures or status epilepticus with encephalopathy. Outside the reviewed evidence, the committee was aware that antibody-guided immunotherapy may improve outcomes compared with standard antiseizure medication. Evidence concerning 'autoimmune epilepsy' is emerging, and effective immunomodulation strategies for defined autoimmune epilepsy syndromes remain a research question. Suspected autoimmune encephalitis is relatively rare; testing for it already occurs in practice.

document_sections.heading: Information and support
document_sections.content: Evidence identified gaps in communication, information and support. Some people with epilepsy and some parents or carers reported that information was withheld, limiting participation in care. Children and young people wanted involvement but sometimes received information they could not understand, including information about sudden unexpected death in epilepsy (SUDEP). Information should therefore reflect developmental age and individual circumstances; people with learning disabilities or complex needs may need additional consultation time and support. Epilepsy specialist nurses have an important information-giving role. Parents and carers reported difficulty locating support beyond their doctor, so people should be directed to local and national groups and help with daily activities. At the first appointment, discussions about adherence, epilepsy-related risks, seizure triggers and everyday activities, including driving, support self-management; repeat relevant information later. Concerns can change, so offer discussion at every appointment and use commonly raised topics to structure it. The committee considered the recommendations consistent with current practice and did not anticipate substantial resource effects.

document_sections.heading: New technologies
document_sections.content: No evidence was found for digital health technologies, so the committee made no clinical recommendation about their use. People already use devices such as night monitors and alarms for self-management, but supporting evidence is lacking and the NHS does not currently offer them for this purpose. The committee considered that some monitoring tools might help and called for research into their clinical effectiveness and cost effectiveness.

document_sections.heading: Referral to tertiary specialist services
document_sections.content: Because referral evidence was lacking, the committee drew on clinical experience and NHS England 2019 referral-pathway guidance. Tertiary services should be accessible through a specialist whenever needed. People with learning disabilities or mental health problems may need help obtaining referrals or attending appointments, even when another specialist already sees them. More specific criteria should prioritise epilepsy that is difficult to diagnose or manage and allow consideration of clinical trials. People meeting those criteria should be seen within 4 weeks; the committee expected timely care to benefit prognosis without materially changing resources. Children meeting urgent criteria should be seen within 2 weeks. Those under 3 years warrant prompt assessment because some syndromes beginning early carry developmental risks. Myoclonic seizures presenting up to 4 years may indicate a potentially treatable neurodegenerative disorder. A unilateral structural lesion can complicate seizure management and prompt early surgical consideration. Deterioration in behaviour, speech or learning, including loss of acquired milestones, merits prompt investigation, particularly without an established diagnosis. The recommendations reinforce current best practice.

document_sections.heading: Treatment with antiseizure medications
document_sections.content: These general treatment principles reflect the committee's informal consensus and update earlier guidance. Once epilepsy is confirmed, medicine choice should balance benefits and harms against seizure type, circumstances and the person's preferences, through shared decision making in primary, secondary or tertiary care. Cognitive effects, the speed of seizure reduction and life plans may affect priorities. Older people, particularly those with co-occurring conditions, need consideration of drug interactions, starting dose and titration; the NICE multimorbidity guidance may also help. If seizures persist with monotherapy, review the diagnosis and consider another medicine. Increase the new medicine gradually while changing from the existing treatment to limit withdrawal-related effects and establish an appropriate dose. If alternatives fail, consider add-on treatment, titrate carefully and review adverse effects because medicines may interact, including sodium valproate and lamotrigine. Seek the best balance of seizure control and tolerability, and discuss avoiding unnecessary medicines. These recommendations reinforce existing practice rather than changing it.

document_sections.heading: When to start antiseizure medication
document_sections.content: The committee's informal consensus does not support routinely starting antiseizure medication after a first unprovoked seizure. Early treatment may be considered when neurological examination shows a deficit, EEG demonstrates unequivocal epileptic activity, imaging shows a structural brain abnormality, or further seizures present an unacceptable risk to the person or their family or carers. A deficit or epileptic EEG activity may signal greater recurrence risk; circumstances such as possible loss of employment can also influence the decision. Treatment after a structural abnormality may prevent further seizures. The recommendations reinforce current practice.

document_sections.heading: Safety considerations
document_sections.content: The safety recommendations derive from the committee's informal consensus. Because antiseizure medicines differ, follow MHRA advice when switching between manufacturers, generic versions or branded and generic products. Serious complications associated with phenytoin warrant particular awareness for people of Han Chinese or Thai family background; those associated with carbamazepine and potentially structurally similar oxcarbazepine and eslicarbazepine acetate warrant awareness for people of Han Chinese, Thai, European or Japanese family background. Some antiseizure medicines have been commonly reported to reduce bone mineral density and increase osteomalacia risk; consider appropriate supplementation in people at risk. Recommendation 4.3.5 was added in January 2025 after MHRA changes. Its precautionary advice rests on 1 retrospective observational study suggesting a possible increase in neurodevelopmental disorders among children of men treated with valproate in the 3 months before conception compared with children of men treated with lamotrigine or levetiracetam; causality remains unknown. Women and girls need information and regular reviews as circumstances concerning contraception, conception, pregnancy, breastfeeding, childcare and menopause evolve. January 2025 changes aligned sodium valproate and topiramate recommendations with MHRA regulations. For women and girls of childbearing potential, the Pregnancy Prevention Programme conditions address substantial fetal risks and include highly effective contraception, a pregnancy test before starting either medicine and awareness of its risks. In the absence of evidence, the committee supported breastfeeding when desired, judging its benefits to outweigh the small potential medication risk to the child. Reviews may increase because services are thought to be under-commissioned. MHRA advice may prompt some people taking medicines other than lamotrigine and levetiracetam to reconsider treatment.

document_sections.heading: Monitoring and review
document_sections.content: Reviews allow care plans to change with people's needs. Evidence did not suggest a difference in benefits or harms between scheduled and patient-initiated reviews. Patient-initiated review may improve timely access and autonomy but can disadvantage people with less independence or decision-making capacity, allow loss of contact with services or be unsafe for serious or complex conditions. The committee supported patient-initiated access for everyone alongside scheduled reviews for people with reduced decision-making capacity, serious or complex epilepsy, significant comorbidities, or medicines associated with long-term harms or interactions, and for children and young people. Possible long-term harms include changes in blood parameters, bone health and lipid metabolism; enzyme-inducing medicines are particularly associated with lower bone density. Regular review also provides women and girls able to have children who take sodium valproate, topiramate or another high-risk teratogenic medicine an opportunity to discuss options and pregnancy plans. Children and young people typically have 2 reviews a year and at least one every 12 months. Evidence suggested little benefit difference between therapeutic drug monitoring and clinical review. Monitoring drug levels is unnecessary for most people but may help when seizures remain uncontrolled, adverse effects occur, adherence is uncertain, precise titration is needed or pregnancy and comorbidities alter risk; lamotrigine levels may change during pregnancy and after birth. Moving away from routine scheduled reviews for everyone may change practice. Specialist nurse services may need development to coordinate patient-initiated access, although demand is expected to be manageable if higher-need groups retain regular reviews. Targeted drug-level monitoring should not increase provider burden and might slightly reduce it.

document_sections.heading: Support and monitoring
document_sections.content: Evidence for medication-level monitoring in pregnancy came from a single study and was inconclusive. Recommendations therefore draw on clinical experience and MHRA advice concerning carbamazepine, lamotrigine, levetiracetam, oxcarbazepine, phenobarbital and phenytoin during pregnancy. In January 2025, a referral recommendation was added so men taking valproate who plan a family within the next year can discuss potential fertility risks and alternatives with an epilepsy specialist team. Some tertiary centres offer on-site measurements for carbamazepine, phenytoin and phenobarbital; girls and women planning pregnancy do not usually take the latter 2 medicines. On the basis of consensus, consider pre-conception levels for women and girls whose seizures may worsen during pregnancy. A pre-conception value provides a reference for comparing levels and adjusting doses in pregnancy. The committee requested stronger research evidence. Because some women planning pregnancy or already pregnant do not currently undergo drug monitoring, implementing MHRA-aligned advice may increase testing.

document_sections.heading: Discontinuing antiseizure medication
document_sections.content: Withdrawal decisions depend on individual recurrence risk and preferences. Although evidence identified some independent recurrence factors, the committee considered an isolated list potentially misleading. Continue weighing benefits and risks as circumstances change, and assess recurrence risk individually after 2 years without seizures. Discuss the epilepsy type and personal circumstances: juvenile myoclonic epilepsy, structural abnormalities and co-existing neurodegenerative or other neurological conditions can confer substantial recurrence risk after withdrawal. Obtain specialist advice if benefits or risks are uncertain; after epilepsy surgery, withdrawal should be guided by the surgery centre. Reduce medicines slowly, particularly benzodiazepines and barbiturates because withdrawal symptoms can occur, and seek epilepsy specialist guidance if seizures return. These recommendations reinforce existing practice.

document_sections.heading: Generalised tonic-clonic seizures
document_sections.content: These seizures rapidly involve both cerebral hemispheres, causing loss of consciousness followed by muscle stiffening and rhythmic jerking. For time to treatment failure, evidence showed no medicine outperforming sodium valproate; it showed clear advantages over lacosamide, phenobarbital, carbamazepine and topiramate. No clear difference from other medicines was found for remission or time to first seizure. After sodium valproate, lamotrigine and levetiracetam performed next best on time to treatment failure, so the January 2025 update made all 3 first-line monotherapy options subject to MHRA restrictions. Discuss and review reproductive safety measures for women and girls and precautionary advice for boys and men taking sodium valproate. Adverse events were inconsistently reported, limiting comparisons, although careful titration or dose adjustment can manage many events. Evidence could not clearly rank add-on drugs. Lamotrigine, levetiracetam, perampanel and topiramate performed better than placebo for a 50% response rate; clobazam and sodium valproate were included on the basis of experience and established use despite no identified evidence for them. Levetiracetam and perampanel showed some evidence of greater seizure freedom than placebo, with substantial uncertainty. Brivaracetam might outperform placebo for more than 50% seizure-frequency reduction, while lacosamide was less effective than levetiracetam on that outcome. These 2 medicines, alongside phenobarbital, primidone and zonisamide, were included as possible second-line add-ons partly on clinical experience. Topiramate requires Pregnancy Prevention Programme conditions for women and girls of childbearing potential. Some medicines can aggravate absence or myoclonic seizures, including those in juvenile myoclonic epilepsy. Long-term primidone and sodium valproate can lower bone mineral density and increase osteomalacia risk; consider supplementation for those at risk. Prescribing order may change, and sodium valproate or topiramate may require extra counselling, clinical assessment and administration.

document_sections.heading: Focal seizures with or without evolution to bilateral tonic-clonic seizures
document_sections.content: Focal seizures begin in 1 area on 1 side of the brain, with awareness preserved or impaired; manifestations depend on their origin. Lamotrigine and levetiracetam were continued longer than other medicines in studies of focal epilepsy, suggesting possible effectiveness and tolerability advantages. They were not more effective for remission at 6 and 12 months, however, and appeared less effective than carbamazepine for time to first seizure. Lamotrigine, levetiracetam and gabapentin may have more tolerable adverse events, but inconsistent reporting limits comparisons; titration and dose changes may manage many effects. Evidence and economic modelling supported lamotrigine and levetiracetam as first-line monotherapies, followed by carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine or zonisamide, then lacosamide because its evidence was weaker. For add-on therapy, evidence could not clearly identify the best medicine. Brivaracetam, carbamazepine, eslicarbazepine acetate, lacosamide, lamotrigine, levetiracetam, oxcarbazepine, perampanel, pregabalin, topiramate and zonisamide were effective compared with placebo for more than 50% seizure-frequency reduction; medicines with the strongest evidence became first-line add-ons. Cenobamate was included after at least 1 unsuccessful add-on medicine in accordance with NICE technology appraisal guidance. Add-on adverse-event data were too inconsistent to guide ranking. Sodium valproate was moved to third-line add-on therapy in January 2025; phenobarbital, phenytoin and vigabatrin were reserved for earlier treatments that fail or cannot be tolerated. Observe MHRA reproductive precautions for sodium valproate and Pregnancy Prevention Programme conditions for topiramate. Serious complications associated with phenytoin warrant attention in people of Han Chinese or Thai family background, and those associated with carbamazepine and possibly oxcarbazepine or eslicarbazepine acetate in people of Han Chinese, Thai, European or Japanese family background. Long-term carbamazepine, phenytoin and sodium valproate may harm bone health; consider supplementation for those at risk. Recommendations largely reinforce practice, though levetiracetam use may rise slightly without significantly increasing costs, and add-on prescribing order may change. Gabapentin and clobazam are no longer recommended as add-ons here; use may fall slightly, although people doing well on them are likely to continue.

document_sections.heading: Absence seizures
document_sections.content: Absence seizures are generalised events involving impaired awareness, cessation of activity or speech, and blank staring. They can occur alone or in childhood absence epilepsy, juvenile absence epilepsy or juvenile myoclonic epilepsy. Treatment evidence concerned children and young people; the committee extrapolated it to adults because pathophysiology is similar. Limited evidence suggests ethosuximide may improve absence-seizure outcomes and remission, and it may benefit cognition; clinical experience supports its first-line use. Sodium valproate may increase remission and appeared to produce fewer adverse events than other reviewed medicines. Lamotrigine and levetiracetam also appeared effective. Following January 2025 MHRA changes, all 3 are second-line monotherapy or add-on options for absence seizures, with sodium valproate reproductive precautions. Long-term sodium valproate can lower bone mineral density and increase osteomalacia risk; consider supplementation in those at risk. Some other medicines may aggravate seizures. For absence seizures accompanied by, or at risk of, other seizure types, evidence linked sodium valproate to greater remission and good tolerability. After the January 2025 update, sodium valproate, levetiracetam and lamotrigine are all first-line monotherapy or add-on options, subject to sodium valproate precautions. Ethosuximide may improve absence outcomes and remission and is a possible second-line add-on, but should not be the sole medicine when other seizure types coexist because it controls only absence seizures. For some women and girls able to have children, sodium valproate remains an option only after thorough discussion, unsuccessful alternatives and adherence to MHRA safety advice through shared decision making. Prescribing order may change and sodium valproate requires additional counselling, clinical assessment and administration.

document_sections.heading: Myoclonic seizures
document_sections.content: First-line evidence was very limited, so clinical expertise and opinion informed recommendations. Onset before 4 years may indicate an underlying neurodegenerative disorder and warrants tertiary paediatric neurology involvement. Myoclonic seizures are generalised; because direct first-line and monotherapy evidence was absent, the committee drew on generalised tonic-clonic seizure evidence. It judged sodium valproate the most effective option relative to other antiseizure medicines, while levetiracetam was also effective. Both became first-line monotherapy or add-on options in January 2025, subject to MHRA sodium valproate precautions. Long-term sodium valproate can reduce bone mineral density and increase osteomalacia risk; consider supplementation for those at risk. For some women and girls able to have children, sodium valproate may remain an option after thorough discussion, unsuccessful alternatives, MHRA safeguards, shared decision making and independent assessment and agreement by a second specialist. Without robust evidence, the committee identified brivaracetam, clobazam, clonazepam, lamotrigine, phenobarbital, piracetam, topiramate and zonisamide as possible second-line choices; selection depends on clinical factors and preferences. Topiramate requires Pregnancy Prevention Programme conditions in women and girls of childbearing potential. Lamotrigine can sometimes aggravate myoclonic seizures. Carbamazepine, gabapentin, oxcarbazepine, phenytoin, pregabalin, tiagabine and vigabatrin should not be used because they increase seizure frequency. Treatment order may change, and sodium valproate may require additional counselling, clinical assessment and administration.

document_sections.heading: Tonic or atonic seizures
document_sections.content: Atonic loss of tone or sustained tonic stiffening can cause a sudden fall. These seizures occur in Lennox–Gastaut syndrome and other conditions, often cause injury and can substantially affect quality of life. Assessment by a neurologist with epilepsy expertise helps establish the syndrome and guide investigations and treatment. Direct first-line evidence was absent, so the committee extrapolated from generalised tonic-clonic seizures. It judged sodium valproate the most effective option relative to other antiseizure medicines. Following January 2025 MHRA changes, sodium valproate and lamotrigine are first-line monotherapy or add-on options, with reproductive precautions for sodium valproate. Long-term sodium valproate may reduce bone mineral density and raise osteomalacia risk; consider supplementation for those at risk. Evidence supports add-on lamotrigine for seizure or drop-attack control, making it an option for women and girls able to have children. Sodium valproate may still be an option for some of them only after thorough risk–benefit discussion, unsuccessful alternatives, MHRA safeguards and shared decision making. Evidence indicates that clobazam, rufinamide and topiramate may also help as second-line monotherapy or add-ons; no clear cost-effectiveness evidence established one as superior. Topiramate requires Pregnancy Prevention Programme conditions for women and girls of childbearing potential. Low-quality evidence without direct comparisons prevented clear prioritisation of further options. A ketogenic diet may be considered as an add-on under a ketogenic diet team; felbamate may be considered subsequently under an epilepsy-expert neurologist. Some other antiseizure medicines may worsen seizures. Prescribing order may change, and sodium valproate or topiramate may require additional counselling, clinical assessment and administration.

document_sections.heading: Idiopathic generalised epilepsies
document_sections.content: Idiopathic generalised epilepsies are among the most common epilepsy forms. Onset is usually during adolescence but can occur in childhood. Seizures may persist into middle age and then remit in some people, without a way to predict who will remit. Many achieve good seizure control with medicines; the treatment goal is seizure freedom. Evidence identified sodium valproate as the most effective medicine compared with other antiseizure options, some benefit from add-on levetiracetam versus placebo, and fewer treatment-stopping adverse effects and better health-related quality of life with lamotrigine than sodium valproate. In January 2025, sodium valproate, lamotrigine and levetiracetam became first-line monotherapy or add-on options, with MHRA reproductive precautions for sodium valproate. Long-term sodium valproate can reduce bone mineral density and increase osteomalacia risk; consider supplementation for those at risk. Lamotrigine and levetiracetam reduce seizures and are options for women and girls able to have children and younger girls whose epilepsy may continue beyond puberty. Some women and girls able to have children may use sodium valproate only after thorough discussion, unsuccessful alternatives, MHRA safeguards and shared decision making. Studies did not show a clinically important benefit for topiramate against placebo or valproate, although the committee considered it useful in practice. Add-on perampanel reduced seizures. Perampanel and topiramate are second-line add-on options; topiramate requires Pregnancy Prevention Programme conditions in women and girls of childbearing potential. Prescribing order may change and sodium valproate or topiramate may require additional counselling, clinical assessment and administration.

document_sections.heading: Dravet syndrome
document_sections.content: Dravet syndrome usually begins in the first year of life with prolonged febrile seizures that can require intensive care. Diagnosis may be difficult during that year; these treatment recommendations apply after confirmation and discussion with a paediatric neurologist. Response is variable and management is complex, warranting an epilepsy-expert neurologist. With no direct first-line evidence, the committee used experience to support sodium valproate for seizure reduction despite its risks and limited alternatives, often starting treatment under 2 years. Discuss benefits and risks, follow MHRA safeguards and use caution. Long-term sodium valproate may reduce bone mineral density and increase osteomalacia risk; consider supplementation for those at risk. Limited evidence suggested that sodium valproate, clobazam and stiripentol together reduced seizures in children and young people previously treated unsuccessfully with clobazam and sodium valproate. The committee supported this first-line add-on approach with careful titration and regular review for effects such as sedation. NICE technology appraisal guidance supports cannabidiol with clobazam as a second-line option. Evidence was absent for further treatment when seizures persist; specialist- or ketogenic-team-supervised options rely on experience and expert opinion. Potassium bromide is seldom used but may help some people. Further research is needed when first-line treatment fails or cannot be tolerated. Recommendations reinforce best practice.

document_sections.heading: Lennox–Gastaut syndrome
document_sections.content: Lennox–Gastaut syndrome is a severe childhood-onset developmental and epileptic encephalopathy. Diagnosis can be difficult, and antiseizure treatment may begin before confirmation. Treatment responses vary and epilepsy-expert neurology involvement is needed. No first-line treatment evidence was available; clinical experience supported cautious first-line sodium valproate because effective alternatives are few and treatment often starts under 2 years. Discuss benefits and risks and follow MHRA safeguards. Long-term sodium valproate can lower bone mineral density and increase osteomalacia risk; consider supplementation for those at risk. Evidence found add-on lamotrigine effective against seizures and drop attacks, supporting its second-line use as an add-on or monotherapy when first-line treatment fails or is intolerable. When added to sodium valproate, use a lower starting dose and cautious titration because the medicines interact. Some evidence suggested that clobazam, rufinamide and topiramate add-ons reduced seizure frequency and drop attacks versus placebo. NICE technology appraisal guidance also supports cannabidiol with clobazam as a later option. Topiramate requires Pregnancy Prevention Programme conditions for women and girls of childbearing potential. Robust evidence for still later treatment was absent; a ketogenic diet or felbamate may be considered under the appropriate specialist team. Other medicines used in practice may worsen seizures in some people. Limited published trial data motivated a research recommendation for treatment after unsuccessful or intolerable first-line therapy. The recommendations mainly reinforce existing practice.

document_sections.heading: Infantile spasms syndrome
document_sections.content: Infantile spasms are a severe developmental and epileptic encephalopathy requiring urgent care and immediate tertiary paediatric neurology guidance. Untreated spasms risk poor long-term neurodevelopment, whereas prompt diagnosis and treatment are associated with better prognosis. Monitor during and after therapy for recurrent spasms, new seizure types and treatment harms. Evidence suggested that steroids combined with vigabatrin stop spasms more effectively than either treatment alone. Evidence did not clearly favour oral over injected steroids, but the committee considered oral treatment easier. Steroids may be unsuitable for some children under 2 years, including those with neurological impairments or other comorbidities; consider vigabatrin alone when steroid adverse-effect risk is high. Evidence supported vigabatrin alone initially for spasms associated with tuberous sclerosis, adding high-dose oral prednisolone if it is ineffective after 1 week. Discuss steroid effects with parents and carers, including infection, high blood pressure and high blood glucose, and explain reducing exposure to infections such as chickenpox and responding to possible exposure. Higher doses of vigabatrin and oral steroids improved freedom from spasms in the reviewed evidence; increase doses in accordance with BNF for children. Vigabatrin above specified doses may be needed if spasms persist, but only with specialist supervision. Robust second-line evidence is absent, so subsequent options rely on specialist experience. The lack of controlled trial data after first-line failure prompted a research recommendation. The recommendations reinforce best practice.

document_sections.heading: Self-limited epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes
document_sections.content: Children generally outgrow this syndrome by their early teens. Some have infrequent seizures with little effect on wellbeing, so treatment is not always chosen. Discuss treatment versus no treatment, seizure hazards, adverse effects and the very rare risk of SUDEP. The committee considered current antiseizure treatment effective in practice. Direct medicine evidence was limited; because seizures are usually focal, first- and second-line options were informed by focal-epilepsy studies. Those studies found longer continuation of lamotrigine and levetiracetam, suggesting possible effectiveness and tolerability benefits, but no greater remission at 6 and 12 months and a less favourable time to first seizure than carbamazepine. Lamotrigine, levetiracetam and gabapentin may have more tolerable adverse events, although inconsistent reporting limits comparisons. The committee supported lamotrigine and levetiracetam first, followed by carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine or zonisamide as second-line monotherapy. Carbamazepine and potentially similar oxcarbazepine and eslicarbazepine acetate carry particular serious-complication risks for people of Han Chinese, Thai, European or Japanese family background. Long-term carbamazepine may reduce bone mineral density and increase osteomalacia risk; consider supplementation for those at risk. Evidence showed seizure reduction with sulthiame, but its limited evidence and licensing position led the committee to place it third-line after licensed choices, following tertiary paediatric neurology discussion. A November 2025 note states that sulthiame is now licensed in the UK and recommendations 6.4.2 to 6.4.4 are under review. In a small number of children, carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine or lamotrigine may increase seizures or coincide with another syndrome. Concerning changes should prompt sleep EEG to exclude developmental epileptic encephalopathy with spike-wave activation in sleep; poor school performance should prompt neuropsychology assessment. Tailor reviews to seizure frequency, treatment and other needs, and discuss withdrawal after 2 seizure-free years or at age 14 years. Recommendations mainly reinforce existing practice.

document_sections.heading: Epilepsy with myoclonic-atonic seizures (Doose syndrome)
document_sections.content: This is a rare condition of young children for which accurate diagnosis and tertiary paediatric neurology advice are important. No treatment evidence was identified. Clinical experience supported levetiracetam and sodium valproate as first-line possibilities because they are used effectively for generalised epilepsy, including this syndrome. Sodium valproate needs caution, full benefit–risk discussion, MHRA safeguards and regular reassessment; the committee retained it as an option because alternatives are limited, treatment often starts young and most children outgrow seizures by their teenage years. Long-term sodium valproate may reduce bone mineral density and increase osteomalacia risk; consider supplementation for those at risk. Studies known to the committee and clinical experience supported a ketogenic diet as second-line alternative or add-on under a ketogenic diet team. In the absence of evidence, clinical experience identified clobazam, ethosuximide, topiramate and zonisamide as possible choices only after earlier options fail. Topiramate requires Pregnancy Prevention Programme conditions for women and girls of childbearing potential. Do not use carbamazepine, gabapentin, oxcarbazepine, phenytoin, pregabalin or vigabatrin because they increase seizure frequency in this syndrome. Consider withdrawing treatment after 2 seizure-free years in children. Further research is needed when first-line therapy fails or is intolerable. Major practice change is not expected.

document_sections.heading: Status epilepticus
document_sections.content: Convulsive status epilepticus requires immediate emergency antiseizure treatment. Follow an available individual emergency plan specifying the prescribed rescue medicine, trained administrator and timing. Evidence favoured benzodiazepines overall without clearly identifying a superior one; rapid delivery matters more than which benzodiazepine is selected. Buccal or rectal administration is usual in the community when intravenous access is unavailable. Intravenous lorazepam is the hospital first choice because of rapid action and less respiratory depression and sedation than alternatives. Buccal midazolam remains the community first choice; rectal diazepam can substitute according to previous use or availability. After 2 benzodiazepine doses, evidence supports intravenous levetiracetam, phenytoin or valproate without showing an efficacy advantage for 1. Levetiracetam may be prepared and administered more quickly and may cause fewer adverse effects; another second-line medicine can be considered if the initial one fails. January 2025 MHRA sodium valproate safeguards also apply to intravenous use. Limited evidence supported phenobarbital or general anaesthesia as third-line options under expert guidance. Some causes require additional treatment, and non-epileptic attacks need to be distinguished from convulsive status epilepticus. Recommendations reflect current practice and are not expected to have a substantial resource effect.

document_sections.heading: Repeated or cluster seizures
document_sections.content: Treatment evidence was limited. Some evidence supported benzodiazepines, with clobazam and midazolam given as examples from current practice; rectal diazepam is less preferred because of its administration route. The committee requested further studies using clear, consistent definitions of repeated or cluster seizures. Recommendations reflect current practice without an expected substantial resource effect.

document_sections.heading: Prolonged seizures
document_sections.content: No evidence was found for treating prolonged convulsive seizures, described here as lasting less than 5 minutes but more than 2 minutes beyond the person's usual seizure. The former definition included seizures longer than 5 minutes when status epilepticus required persistence for 30 minutes; the revised ILAE definition classifies seizures lasting longer than 5 minutes as status epilepticus. Prolonged convulsive seizures require emergency management. Clinical experience supported benzodiazepines as an option, with midazolam commonly used. Recommendations align with current practice and are not expected to have a substantial resource effect.

document_sections.heading: Ketogenic diet
document_sections.content: Available evidence did not establish clear benefits of ketogenic diets for adults or children with drug-resistant epilepsy. The committee also noted potential long-term health drawbacks and high delivery costs. Clinical experience nevertheless suggested occasional benefit for a small number of people, including children with certain syndromes. The committee did not recommend routine use but retained the diet for specialist consideration when few other options remain. It requested stronger evidence about effectiveness and long-term tolerability. Because ketogenic diets are not routinely offered, little effect on present practice is expected.

document_sections.heading: Resective epilepsy surgery
document_sections.content: Evidence indicated that resective surgery is the most clinically effective treatment for drug-resistant focal epilepsy in children, young people and adults, with better quality of life and less recurrence than medical care. Surgery also produced more postoperative cognitive deficits and other adverse events. The committee judged benefits to outweigh harms: cognitive changes often did not substantially impair everyday function, and perioperative infection, bleeding or postoperative mood changes were often self-limiting. Surgical harms must also be weighed against injury, head injury and SUDEP from ongoing seizures. Risk may rise with surgical complexity, but the overall favourable balance was considered likely across most surgery types and ages. Health economic modelling found surgery cost effective in adults; data were insufficient to model children. The committee judged cost effectiveness highly likely in children because outcomes tend to be better and benefits last longer, although assessment can cost more. No evidence established optimal referral criteria. The committee supported referral for consideration of surgery for everyone with drug-resistant epilepsy, including those without identified MRI abnormalities, and early tertiary referral at diagnosis when particular MRI abnormalities suggest future drug resistance. Learning disabilities or genetic abnormalities should not exclude indicated assessment. Currently only a proportion of eligible people are referred, amid limited surgery provision and long waits. Wider referral will probably increase presurgical investigations and operations and may require more training and investment. Early referral before drug resistance may add a relatively small tertiary-service burden.

document_sections.heading: Vagus nerve stimulation
document_sections.content: Robust long-term evidence for vagus nerve stimulation was absent. Use varies and is generally considered when medicines have not controlled seizures and resective surgery is unsuitable or unsuccessful. No evidence warranted removing it as an option for this small group with complex needs, but it does not help everyone and has procedural risks; discuss benefits and harms before a shared decision. NICE has related interventional guidance for children with refractory epilepsy. The committee requested research into effectiveness. The recommendations are unlikely to greatly change practice.

document_sections.heading: Psychological, neurobehavioural, cognitive and developmental comorbidities in epilepsy
document_sections.content: Mental health conditions, learning disabilities and dementia are more prevalent among people with epilepsy. Gaps in communication between specialties support continuing multidisciplinary coordination with people and, where appropriate, families or carers. These coordination recommendations reflect good practice but will change routine practice for most providers. Psychological-treatment studies differed in intervention, provider and population. Those differences did not significantly change the epilepsy-related quality-of-life outcome, but pooled evidence could not support particular interventions for particular subgroups. Evidence for children and young people was extremely limited and very uncertain; complex childhood syndromes may require additional multidisciplinary neurodevelopmental support. Without health economic evidence, the committee could not confidently recommend tailored psychological interventions and called for cost-effectiveness research. Depression is more frequent in epilepsy; anxiety is associated with it and psychosis to a lesser extent. Suicide mortality risk is also increased. Review for psychological difficulties and use existing NICE depression guidance. Access to psychological services, especially for children and young people, varies and waiting lists can be long. Highlighting existing guidance may improve access, without an expected significant resource effect from support and treatment recommendations.

document_sections.heading: Reducing the risk of epilepsy-related death including sudden unexpected death in epilepsy
document_sections.content: Evidence was insufficient to recommend tools predicting SUDEP or other epilepsy-related deaths. Sparse SUDEP-7 and SUDEP-7 revised data suggested good accuracy but had very high imprecision because few SUDEP events occurred. Evidence for 3 all-cause mortality tools came from a single study with insufficient data. The committee requested development and validation of a broader death-risk tool covering causes such as suicide, injury and drowning, supported by long-running, detailed national or international registries. It also suggested larger, nearer-term validation of SUDEP-7. The estimated lifetime SUDEP risk is between 7% and 12%; it is higher with severe drug-resistant epilepsy, particularly uncontrolled tonic-clonic seizures. Discuss each person's risk and ways to reduce it. Important potentially modifiable factors include medication non-adherence, alcohol or drug misuse, living or sleeping alone without supervision, and generalised tonic-clonic, focal to bilateral tonic-clonic or uncontrolled seizures. Adherence and seizure control can significantly reduce seizure-related death risk; lack of adherence can also increase seizure frequency and injury. Living or sleeping alone without supervision increased mortality risk in the reviewed evidence, although night supervision may not be feasible for adults living independently and no approach removes every risk. Clinical history should also consider abnormal neurological findings, neurological conditions and cancer, alongside other individual risks. Evidence for interventions preventing seizure-related death, including SUDEP, was limited. Evidence specifically supporting nocturnal supervision was too sparse or weak for a firm recommendation, but some suggested benefit; discuss it and other practical measures with people having sleep-related seizures, including adherence and sleep hygiene. Families may consider a monitor or sharing a room. Supporting prescribed medicine use is especially important for generalised tonic-clonic or focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizures. The recommendations should make risk conversations more consistent; discussing night-time supervision reflects current good practice.

document_sections.heading: Epilepsy specialist nurses
document_sections.content: Clinical evidence on epilepsy specialist nurses was limited in quality and quantity, partly because funding and randomised research are difficult where nurses are already embedded in services. Economic evidence suggested savings over the long term and within the first year, supporting access for people with epilepsy. Specialist nurses provide information, medication and adverse-effect advice, care planning and help with daily life while supporting other professionals and services; they may identify previously unrecognised long-standing adverse effects. Evidence supported sessions addressing emotional wellbeing and self-management. Needs change over time and ongoing seizures may require more contact. Economic evidence suggested nurse-led care can save costs and be cost effective when provided twice a year and after an emergency department visit; the committee recommended this for people with ongoing seizures or following such a visit. This group, approximately 300,000 people in England, is broader than that in the economic analyses. A quarter have at least 1 emergency department visit per year, and nearly all have some hospital outpatient contact, so many nurse appointments may already occur or replace other appointments. Additional appointments are expected, but their increase should be much smaller than if offered to everyone, with costs potentially recovered within the first year. Availability varies; some services may need nurses or different working arrangements. Expected advantages include greater consistency, access, satisfaction and emotional wellbeing, with possible savings through fewer emergency visits and shorter subsequent hospital stays.

document_sections.heading: Transition from children's to adults' epilepsy services
document_sections.content: Much of existing NICE transition guidance also applies to young people with epilepsy; the committee examined epilepsy-specific themes not covered there. Transition should be individually tailored and jointly planned by paediatric and adult multidisciplinary teams with the young person and, when appropriate, family or carers. Review diagnosis and management together. Evidence suggested multidisciplinary engagement helps young people communicate needs and feel more confident. Transition may be distressing; young people and families have reported unclear information, including about SUDEP and unplanned pregnancy. Provide balanced information about relevant concerns, including stigma, which can affect daily activities, education and engagement with care. Repeat information at intervals in an accessible, developmentally suitable format using understandable language. Young people with learning disabilities and their parents often struggle with poorly planned or late transitions and difficulty understanding service changes. Start planning earlier for complex health or social needs, uncontrolled seizures or learning disabilities, allowing time to arrange support; individual circumstances determine timing and other specialties may need involvement. The committee expected no resource impact because the recommendations reflect best practice.

document_sections.heading: Update information
document_sections.content: In January 2025, recommendations concerning valproate and topiramate were amended to align with MHRA guidance. Valproate must not be started for the first time in anyone younger than 55 years unless 2 specialists independently judge and document that no effective, tolerated alternative exists or compelling reasons make reproductive risks inapplicable. Boys and men should be advised to use effective contraception—condoms plus contraception used by a female sexual partner—during valproate treatment and for 3 months after stopping. Men taking valproate who plan a family within the next year should discuss potential fertility risks and treatment options with a healthcare professional. Topiramate should not be used in women or girls of childbearing potential unless Pregnancy Prevention Programme conditions are met. The guideline replaced CG137 in April 2022. A November 2025 update added links to relevant technology appraisal guidance for childhood-onset epilepsies; other minor updates added links to MHRA advice on valproate and topiramate and to NICE guidance on adrenal insufficiency.
